cues.prompt: In this example, gas costs \$1.459 per litre. How many litres can you buy with \$50? Round to the nearest tenth.
cues.working: You know dollars and the rate is dollars per litre, so divide: \$50 ÷ \$1.459 per litre ≈ $34.3$ L. B multiplies instead.

m202-8-2-b.title: Solving Problems with Rates, Part 2: Changing Units Along the Way

cues.prompt: In this example, a car uses $6.5$ L/100 km and gas costs \$1.52 per litre. How much does the gas cost for a $300$ km trip?
cues.working: $300$ km is $3$ hundreds, so the car uses $3 \times 6.5 = 19.5$ L. The cost is $19.5 \times 1.52 =$ \$29.64. B forgets that the rate is per $100$ km.

m202-8-2-c.title: Solving Problems with Rates, Part 3: Combining Rates and Average Speed

chapters.title: Average speed for a whole trip

cues.prompt: You drive $100$ km at $50$ km/h, then $100$ km at $100$ km/h. What is your average speed for the whole trip?
cues.working: The times are $100 \div 50 = 2$ h and $100 \div 100 = 1$ h, so you drive $200$ km in $3$ h: $200 \div 3 \approx 66.7$ km/h. B is the mean of the speeds.

cues.prompt: A table $2.4$ m long is drawn $8$ cm long. What scale factor was used?
cues.working: $2.4$ m $= 240$ cm, so $k = \dfrac{8}{240} = \dfrac{1}{30}$, a reduction. B divides $8 \div 2.4$ without converting.

m202-8-3-b.title: Scale Diagrams, Part 2: Scales Written as Ratios

cues.prompt: On a $1 : 25\,000$ map, a lake is $4.2$ cm across. How wide is the real lake?

m202-8-3-c.title: Scale Diagrams, Part 3: Finding and Choosing a Scale

cues.prompt: Two lakes are $3.6$ km apart. On a map, they are $4.8$ cm apart. What is the scale of the map?
cues.working: $3.6$ km $= 360\,000$ cm, so $n = \dfrac{360\,000}{4.8} = 75\,000$. D divides $4.8 \div 3.6$ without converting.

m202-8-4.title: Similar Objects: Length, Area and Volume, Part 1: Areas Grow by k²

chapters.title: Why area grows by k squared

cues.prompt: Two triangles are similar with scale factor $k = 4$. The small triangle has an area of $5\ \text{cm}^2$. What is the area of the large triangle?
cues.working: Areas are multiplied by $k^2 = 16$, so the area is $5 \times 16 = 80\ \text{cm}^2$. B multiplies by $k$, and C by $k^3$.

m202-8-4-b.title: Similar Objects: Length, Area and Volume, Part 2: Volumes Grow by k³

chapters.title: Why volume grows by k cubed

cues.prompt: A small box holds $3$ L. A similar box has every length twice as long. How much does it hold?
cues.working: Capacity is a volume, so multiply by $k^3 = 2^3 = 8$: $3 \times 8 = 24$ L. B multiplies by $k$, and C by $k^2$.

m202-8-4-c.title: Similar Objects: Length, Area and Volume, Part 3: Working Back to the Scale Factor

chapters.title: From volumes to a surface area

cues.prompt: Two similar boxes have volumes of $27\ \text{cm}^3$ and $125\ \text{cm}^3$. The small box has a surface area of $54\ \text{cm}^2$. What is the surface area of the large box?
cues.working: $k^3 = \dfrac{125}{27}$, so $k = \dfrac{5}{3}$ and $k^2 = \dfrac{25}{9}$. $54 \times \dfrac{25}{9} = 150\ \text{cm}^2$. B multiplies by the volume ratio.

m202-9-1.title: Planning a Research Project, Part 1: A Good Research Question

cues.prompt: Which is the best research question?
choices: Is there a relationship between daily screen time and hours of sleep for students in our grade?
How many people own a phone?
cues.working: A is focused, measurable and neutral. B asks for an opinion, C assumes the answer, and D is answered by a single fact.

m202-9-1-b.title: Planning a Research Project, Part 2: Data, Sources and Fair Questions

cues.prompt: Which survey question is **not** biased?
choices: How many hours of homework do you do on a typical school night?
Don’t you agree that we get too much homework?
Most students think homework is useless. Do you?
Is the pointless homework load too heavy?
cues.working: A asks for a number without suggesting an answer. B opens with “Don’t you agree”, C tells people what others think, and D uses the loaded word “pointless”.

m202-9-1-c.title: Planning a Research Project, Part 3: Fair Samples

cues.prompt: To learn how Albertans feel about a new park, a researcher surveys only people walking in the park. What kind of bias is this?
cues.working: People already using the park are not typical of all Albertans, so the sample does not represent the population.

m202-9-1-d.title: Planning a Research Project, Part 4: From Plan to Presentation

cues.prompt: Jordan’s plan: “Question: Do students who play sports have higher average marks? Data: a survey of $50$ randomly chosen students at my school. Presentation: a poster.” Which part of the plan is missing?
choices: how the data will be collected
cues.working: The plan has a question, data and collection (a random survey) and a presentation, but it never says how the data will be analyzed, for example by comparing the mean marks of the two groups.

cues.prompt: A ramp rises $20$ cm over a horizontal run of $3$ m. What is its slope?
cues.working: $3$ m $= 300$ cm, so the slope is $\dfrac{20}{300} = \dfrac{1}{15}$. B mixes centimetres and metres, and C divides the run by the rise.

m203-1-1-b.title: Slope, Part 2: Finding a Missing Rise or Run

chapters.title: How high does the roof rise?
How long must the ramp be?

cues.prompt: In this example, a ramp may have a slope of at most $\dfrac{1}{15}$. It must rise $40$ cm. What is the shortest run it can have?
cues.working: $\text{run} = \dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{slope}} = 40 \div \dfrac{1}{15} = 40 \times 15 = 600$ cm. B divides $40$ by $15$ instead.

cues.prompt: A bike trail climbs $18$ m over a horizontal distance of $240$ m. What is its grade?
cues.working: $\dfrac{18}{240} = 0.075$, and $0.075 \times 100\% = 7.5\%$. B forgets to multiply by $100\%$, and C divides the run by the rise.

m203-1-1-d.title: Slope, Part 4: Roof Pitch and Comparing Slopes

cues.prompt: Which is steepest: a $10\%$ grade, a 2/12 pitch, or a slope of $\dfrac{1}{8}$?
cues.working: As decimals: $0.10$, $2 \div 12 \approx 0.167$ and $1 \div 8 = 0.125$. The 2/12 pitch has the largest slope.

m203-1-2.title: Rate of Change, Part 1: Rate of Change from a Table

cues.prompt: A candle is $24$ cm tall when lit. After $3$ h it is $16.5$ cm tall. What is the rate of change of its height?
cues.working: $\dfrac{16.5 - 24}{3 - 0} = \dfrac{-7.5}{3} = -2.5$ cm/h. The height goes down, so the rate is negative. D divides the wrong way.

m203-1-2-b.title: Rate of Change, Part 2: What the Rate Means

cues.prompt: A plumber charges \$150 for a $2$ h job and \$255 for a $3.5$ h job. What is the rate of change, and what does it mean?
choices: \$70 per hour: each extra hour adds \$70
\$75 per hour: the plumber earns \$75 per job
cues.working: $\dfrac{255 - 150}{3.5 - 2} = \dfrac{105}{1.5} = 70$ dollars per hour. C forgets to divide by the change in time.

m203-1-2-c.title: Rate of Change, Part 3: The Slope of a Line Graph

cues.prompt: A line graph of a hiker’s elevation passes through $(1, 1350)$ and $(4, 1800)$, with time in hours and elevation in metres. What is the rate of change?
cues.working: $\dfrac{1800 - 1350}{4 - 1} = \dfrac{450}{3} = 150$ m/h. B forgets to divide by the change in time.

m203-1-2-d.title: Rate of Change, Part 4: Graphs with Several Pieces

cues.prompt: A graph of water in a rain barrel has three pieces: $0$ to $2$ h rises from $20$ L to $80$ L, $2$ to $5$ h is flat, and $5$ to $6$ h falls to $30$ L. Which piece changes fastest?
choices: They all change at the same rate.
cues.working: First: $\dfrac{80 - 20}{2} = 30$ L/h. Flat: $0$. Last: $\dfrac{30 - 80}{1} = -50$ L/h. The size $50$ is the largest.

m203-1-3.title: Proportions and Unit Analysis, Part 1: Setting Up a Proportion

cues.prompt: A recipe uses $3$ cups of flour for every $2$ dozen cookies. How much flour is needed for $7$ dozen cookies?
cues.working: $\dfrac{3 \text{ cups}}{2 \text{ dozen}} = \dfrac{x}{7 \text{ dozen}}$, so $x = \dfrac{3 \times 7}{2} = 10.5$ cups. B flips one ratio.

m203-1-3-b.title: Proportions and Unit Analysis, Part 2: Rounding Up and Conversion Factors

cues.prompt: A bag of grass seed covers $45$ m². How many bags are needed for a $310$ m² yard?
cues.working: $\dfrac{310}{45} \approx 6.89$. Six bags are not enough, so buy $7$.

m203-1-3-c.title: Proportions and Unit Analysis, Part 3: Chains of Conversion Factors

cues.prompt: A conveyor belt moves at $15$ m/s. What is its speed in km/h?
cues.working: $\dfrac{15\text{ m}}{1\text{ s}} \times \dfrac{1\text{ km}}{1000\text{ m}} \times \dfrac{3600\text{ s}}{1\text{ h}} = \dfrac{15 \times 3600}{1000} = 54$ km/h.

m203-2-1.title: Surface Area, Part 1: Nets and Rectangular Prisms

chapters.title: Only the faces the job needs

cues.prompt: An open-top planter box is $4$ ft long, $2$ ft wide and $1$ ft high. How much wood covers its outside faces?
cues.working: Bottom: $4 \times 2 = 8$. Front and back: $2 \times 4 \times 1 = 8$. Ends: $2 \times 2 \times 1 = 4$. $8 + 8 + 4 = 20\ \text{ft}^2$. B includes a top.

cues.prompt: A closed wedge is a triangular prism $10$ cm long. Its ends are right triangles with legs $6$ cm and $8$ cm and hypotenuse $10$ cm. What is its surface area?
cues.working: Ends: $2 \times \tfrac12 \times 6 \times 8 = 48$. Rectangles: $(6 + 8 + 10) \times 10 = 240$. $48 + 240 = 288\ \text{cm}^2$. B forgets the ends.

cues.prompt: A closed can has a diameter of $10$ cm and a height of $12$ cm. What is its surface area, to the nearest square centimetre?
cues.working: $r = 5$. $2\pi(5)^2 + 2\pi(5)(12) = 50\pi + 120\pi = 170\pi \approx 534\ \text{cm}^2$. B uses the diameter as the radius.

m203-2-2.title: Surface Area of Pyramids, Cones and Spheres, Part 1: Pyramids

chapters.title: The net of a square pyramid

cues.prompt: A gazebo roof is a square pyramid with a base side of $12$ ft and a slant height of $10$ ft. How much roofing covers the four faces?
cues.working: A roof has no base: $4 \times \tfrac12 \times 12 \times 10 = 240\ \text{ft}^2$. B adds the base, and C forgets the one half.

m203-2-2-b.title: Surface Area of Pyramids, Cones and Spheres, Part 2: Cones

cues.prompt: A party hat is a cone with no base. Its diameter is $16$ cm and its slant height is $20$ cm. How much paper makes the hat, to the nearest square centimetre?
cues.working: $r = 8$, so $\pi r s = \pi(8)(20) = 160\pi \approx 503\ \text{cm}^2$. B uses the diameter, and C adds a base.

m203-2-2-c.title: Surface Area of Pyramids, Cones and Spheres, Part 3: Height or Slant Height?

cues.prompt: A cone has a radius of $6$ cm and a height of $8$ cm. What is its slant height?
cues.working: $s = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ cm. B adds the lengths, and D forgets the square root.

m203-2-2-d.title: Surface Area of Pyramids, Cones and Spheres, Part 4: Spheres and Hemispheres

cues.prompt: A solid wooden hemisphere has a radius of $4$ cm. What is its total surface area, to the nearest square centimetre?
cues.working: $3\pi r^2 = 3\pi(4)^2 = 48\pi \approx 151\ \text{cm}^2$. B is the curved part only, and C is a whole sphere.

m203-2-3.title: Surface Area on the Job, Part 1: Converting Square Units

cues.prompt: A room needs $45$ square yards of carpet. How many square feet is that?
cues.working: Square feet are smaller, so multiply by $3 \times 3 = 9$: $45 \times 9 = 405\ \text{ft}^2$. B multiplies by $3$ only.

m203-2-3-b.title: Surface Area on the Job, Part 2: How Much to Buy and What It Costs

cues.prompt: A fence has $620\ \text{ft}^2$ to stain, with two coats. One can covers $250\ \text{ft}^2$. How many cans are needed?
cues.working: Two coats: $620 \times 2 = 1240\ \text{ft}^2$. $1240 \div 250 = 4.96$, so round up to $5$. C forgets the second coat.

m203-2-3-c.title: Surface Area on the Job, Part 3: Composite Objects

cues.prompt: A propane tank is a cylinder $2$ m long with a hemisphere on each end. The radius is $0.5$ m. What is its surface area, to the nearest hundredth of a square metre?
cues.working: Curved side: $2\pi(0.5)(2) = 2\pi$. Two hemispheres make one sphere: $4\pi(0.5)^2 = \pi$. Total $3\pi \approx 9.42\ \text{m}^2$. No flat circles: they are joins.

m203-3-1.title: Volume and Capacity, Part 1: Volume of a Prism

cues.prompt: A concrete pad is $6$ m long, $4$ m wide and $0.15$ m thick. How much concrete does it need?
cues.working: $V = 6 \times 4 \times 0.15 = 3.6\ \text{m}^3$. B is the area of the top, not the volume.

m203-3-1-b.title: Volume and Capacity, Part 2: Triangular and Other Prisms

chapters.title: A pool with a sloping floor

cues.prompt: A wheelchair ramp is a triangular prism. Its side is a right triangle with a run of $3.6$ m and a rise of $0.3$ m, and the ramp is $1.2$ m wide. How much concrete fills it?
cues.working: Side: $\tfrac12 \times 3.6 \times 0.3 = 0.54\ \text{m}^2$. $V = 0.54 \times 1.2 = 0.648\ \text{m}^3$. B forgets the one half.

m203-3-1-c.title: Volume and Capacity, Part 3: Volume and Capacity

cues.prompt: A cooler’s inside is $50$ cm by $30$ cm by $32$ cm. How many litres does it hold?

m203-3-1-d.title: Volume and Capacity, Part 4: Volume of a Cylinder

cues.prompt: A can has a diameter of $8$ cm and a height of $12$ cm. How many millilitres does it hold, to the nearest millilitre?
cues.working: $r = 4$, so $V = \pi(4)^2(12) = 192\pi \approx 603\ \text{cm}^3 = 603$ mL. B squares the diameter.

m203-3-2.title: Volume of Pyramids, Cones and Spheres, Part 1: Pyramids Hold One Third

cues.prompt: A square pyramid has a base side of $6$ m and a height of $10$ m. What is its volume?
cues.working: $V = \tfrac13 \times 36 \times 10 = 120\ \text{m}^3$. B forgets the one third.

m203-3-2-b.title: Volume of Pyramids, Cones and Spheres, Part 2: Cones

chapters.title: Slant height in a volume formula

cues.prompt: A cone-shaped funnel has a radius of $6$ cm and a height of $8$ cm. How much does it hold, to the nearest cubic centimetre?
cues.working: $V = \tfrac13 \pi(6)^2(8) = 96\pi \approx 302\ \text{cm}^3$. B forgets the one third.

m203-3-2-c.title: Volume of Pyramids, Cones and Spheres, Part 3: Spheres and Hemispheres

cues.prompt: A spherical ornament has a radius of $3$ cm. What is its volume, to the nearest tenth of a cubic centimetre?
cues.working: $V = \tfrac43 \pi(3)^3 = 36\pi \approx 113.1\ \text{cm}^3$. B uses the diameter, $6$, in place of the radius. D is a hemisphere.

m203-3-2-d.title: Volume of Pyramids, Cones and Spheres, Part 4: Composite Objects

cues.prompt: A grain silo is a cylinder with a radius of $3$ m and a height of $10$ m, topped with a hemisphere. What is its volume, to the nearest tenth of a cubic metre?
cues.working: Cylinder: $\pi(3)^2(10) = 90\pi$. Hemisphere: $\tfrac23 \pi(3)^3 = 18\pi$. Total $108\pi \approx 339.3\ \text{m}^3$. B uses a whole sphere, and C leaves out the top.

m203-3-3.title: Volume on the Job, Part 1: Converting Cubic Units

cues.prompt: A trench needs $135\ \text{ft}^3$ of gravel. How many cubic yards is that?
cues.working: Cubic yards are bigger, so divide by $27$: $135 \div 27 = 5\ \text{yd}^3$. B divides by $3$, and C by $9$.

m203-3-3-b.title: Volume on the Job, Part 2: Concrete, Water and Fuel

cues.prompt: A sidewalk section is $10$ m long, $1.5$ m wide and $8$ cm thick. How much concrete does it need?
cues.working: $8$ cm $= 0.08$ m, so $V = 10 \times 1.5 \times 0.08 = 1.2\ \text{m}^3$. B forgets to convert the thickness.

m203-3-3-c.title: Volume on the Job, Part 3: Loads, Trips and Time

cues.prompt: A job needs $52\ \text{m}^3$ of gravel. A dump truck carries $12\ \text{m}^3$ per load. How many loads are needed?
cues.working: $52 \div 12 \approx 4.33$. Four loads leave $4\ \text{m}^3$ short, so round up to $5$.

m203-3-3-d.title: Volume on the Job, Part 4: Working Backward to a Missing Length

cues.prompt: A rectangular planter $2$ m long and $0.5$ m wide holds $0.4\ \text{m}^3$ of soil. How deep is the soil?
cues.working: $0.4 = 2 \times 0.5 \times h = 1 \times h$, so $h = 0.4$ m.

m203-4-1.title: Right Triangle Review, Part 1: Naming Sides and the Pythagorean Theorem

chapters.title: A brace for a farm gate
How high does the ladder reach?

cues.prompt: A rectangular field is $80$ m long and $60$ m wide. How long is the path along its diagonal?
cues.working: $c^2 = 80^2 + 60^2 = 6400 + 3600 = 10\,000$, so $c = 100$ m. C subtracts instead of adding.

m203-4-1-b.title: Right Triangle Review, Part 2: Finding a Side with SOH CAH TOA

cues.prompt: A ramp makes an angle of $5^\circ$ with the ground and has a horizontal run of $8$ m. How high does it rise, to the nearest hundredth of a metre?
cues.working: The run is adjacent and the rise is opposite: $\tan 5^\circ = \dfrac{h}{8}$, so $h = 8\tan 5^\circ \approx 0.70$ m. B divides instead of multiplying.

m203-4-1-c.title: Right Triangle Review, Part 3: Finding an Angle

cues.prompt: A $12$ m zip line drops $3$ m from start to finish. What angle does it make with the horizontal, to the nearest tenth of a degree?
cues.working: The drop is opposite and the line is the hypotenuse: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{12} = 0.25$, so $\theta = \sin^{-1}(0.25) \approx 14.5^\circ$. B uses cosine, and C uses tangent.

m203-4-1-d.title: Right Triangle Review, Part 4: Solving a Whole Problem

cues.prompt: A roof has a 4/12 pitch and a rafter run of $12$ ft. How long is each rafter, to the nearest tenth of a foot?
cues.working: The rise is $12 \times \dfrac{4}{12} = 4$ ft, so $L = \sqrt{12^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{160} \approx 12.6$ ft. B adds the rise and the run.

m203-4-2.title: Problems with Two Right Triangles, Part 1: Angles of Elevation and Depression

chapters.title: A truck below a grain elevator

cues.prompt: From the top of a $60$ m cliff, the angle of depression to a canoe is $25^\circ$. How far is the canoe from the base of the cliff?
cues.working: The angle at the canoe is $25^\circ$. $\tan 25^\circ = \dfrac{60}{d}$, so $d = \dfrac{60}{\tan 25^\circ} \approx 128.7$ m. B multiplies instead of dividing.

m203-4-2-b.title: Problems with Two Right Triangles, Part 2: Triangles on Opposite Sides

cues.prompt: Two people stand on opposite sides of a $30$ m flagpole, in line with it. Their angles of elevation to the top are $40^\circ$ and $55^\circ$. How far apart are they?
cues.working: $\dfrac{30}{\tan 40^\circ} \approx 35.75$ and $\dfrac{30}{\tan 55^\circ} \approx 21.01$. Opposite sides, so add: about $56.8$ m. B subtracts.

m203-4-2-c.title: Problems with Two Right Triangles, Part 3: One Triangle Inside the Other

cues.prompt: From $25$ m away, the angle of elevation to the bottom of a flag on a pole is $20^\circ$, and to the top of the flag is $28^\circ$. How tall is the flag?
cues.working: $25\tan 28^\circ \approx 13.29$ and $25\tan 20^\circ \approx 9.10$. Subtract: about $4.2$ m. B adds the two heights.

m203-4-2-d.title: Problems with Two Right Triangles, Part 4: Find the Shared Side First

cues.prompt: From the top of a lighthouse, the angle of depression to a buoy $50$ m from the base is $40^\circ$. A ship in line beyond the buoy is at an angle of depression of $15^\circ$. How far is the ship from the buoy?
cues.working: $h = 50\tan 40^\circ \approx 41.95$ m. Ship: $\dfrac{41.95}{\tan 15^\circ} \approx 156.57$ m from the base. $156.57 - 50 \approx 106.6$ m. B is the distance from the base.

m203-4-3.title: Chains of Right Triangles, Part 1: A Plan and Survey Sightings

cues.prompt: Two stakes are in line with the base of a $40$ m tower. The angles of elevation to the top are $50^\circ$ and $30^\circ$. How far apart are the stakes?
cues.working: $\dfrac{40}{\tan 30^\circ} \approx 69.28$ and $\dfrac{40}{\tan 50^\circ} \approx 33.56$. Subtract: about $35.7$ m.

m203-4-3-b.title: Chains of Right Triangles, Part 2: Roof Trusses

cues.prompt: A truss spans $30$ ft, and its rafters make a $22^\circ$ angle with the bottom chord. How tall is the king post, to the nearest tenth of a foot?
cues.working: Half the span is $15$ ft, adjacent to $22^\circ$: $k = 15\tan 22^\circ \approx 6.06$ ft. B uses the whole span, and C uses sine.

m203-4-3-c.title: Chains of Right Triangles, Part 3: Stairs with a Landing

cues.prompt: Stairs have $17$ cm risers and $28$ cm treads. What angle do they make with the floor, to the nearest tenth of a degree?
cues.working: $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{17}{28}$, so $\alpha \approx 31.3^\circ$. B divides the tread by the riser.

m203-4-3-d.title: Chains of Right Triangles, Part 4: The Diagonal of a Box

cues.prompt: A storage box is $60$ cm long, $40$ cm wide and $30$ cm high. What is the longest straight rod that fits inside, to the nearest centimetre?
cues.working: $p^2 = 60^2 + 40^2 + 30^2 = 3600 + 1600 + 900 = 6100$, so $p \approx 78.1$ cm. B is the floor diagonal only.

m203-5-1.title: Scale Drawings and Models, Part 1: Reading a Scale

chapters.title: Three ways to write a scale

cues.prompt: On a $1 : 200$ site plan, a driveway is $9.5$ cm long. How long is the real driveway?
cues.working: $9.5 \times 200 = 1900$ cm, and $1900 \div 100 = 19$ m. B forgets to convert centimetres to metres.

m203-5-1-b.title: Scale Drawings and Models, Part 2: Drawing Lengths and Imperial Scales

chapters.title: A two-unit scale as a ratio

cues.prompt: A plan uses the scale $1$ cm represents $2$ m. A fence is $13$ m long. How long should it be drawn?
cues.working: From real life to the drawing, divide: $13 \div 2 = 6.5$ cm. B multiplies instead.

m203-5-1-c.title: Scale Drawings and Models, Part 3: Finding the Scale

cues.prompt: A model train car is $16$ cm long. The real car is $13.92$ m long. What is the scale?
cues.working: $13.92$ m $= 1392$ cm, and $1392 \div 16 = 87$, so the scale is $1 : 87$. D has the parts the wrong way round.

m203-5-1-d.title: Scale Drawings and Models, Part 4: Area and Volume with a Scale Factor

cues.prompt: A patio is redesigned with every length $3$ times as long. The old patio used $40$ paving stones. About how many does the new patio need?
cues.working: Area is multiplied by $k^2 = 3^2 = 9$, so it needs about $40 \times 9 = 360$ stones. B multiplies by $k$, and C by $k^3$.

m203-5-2.title: Views of Three-Dimensional Objects, Part 1: Top Views and Counting Cubes

cues.prompt: How many cubes are in the stack shown by this top view?
cues.working: $4 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 13$. B counts the spots, not the cubes.

m203-5-2-b.title: Views of Three-Dimensional Objects, Part 2: Front and Side Views

cues.prompt: What are the column heights of the front view, left to right?
cues.working: Left column: $1$ and $3$, tallest $3$. Right column: $4$ and $2$, tallest $4$. B adds the stacks.

m203-5-2-c.title: Views of Three-Dimensional Objects, Part 3: Isometric Drawings

cues.prompt: A box is $4$ ft long across the front, $2$ ft deep and $3$ ft tall. What is its top view?
cues.working: Looking down, you see the length and the depth: $4$ ft by $2$ ft. B is the front view, and C is the side view.

m203-5-2-d.title: Views of Three-Dimensional Objects, Part 4: Working Backward from Views

chapters.title: Two views are not always enough

cues.prompt: A structure on a $2$ by $2$ base has a front view of two columns, each $2$ tall, and a right side view of two columns, each $2$ tall. What is the most cubes it could have?
cues.working: Every column and every row is $2$ tall, so each of the $4$ spots can hold up to $2$: at most $2 \times 4 = 8$ cubes.

m203-5-3.title: Exploded Views and Components, Part 1: Reading an Exploded View

cues.prompt: An exploded view of a small table shows a top (A), 4 legs (B) and 4 rails (C). Each leg is fastened with 2 screws. How many parts and screws are needed?
cues.working: Parts: $1 + 4 + 4 = 9$. Screws: $4$ legs $\times\ 2 = 8$. B counts the labels, not the parts.

m203-5-3-b.title: Exploded Views and Components, Part 2: Parts Lists and Costs

cues.prompt: A kit needs $6$ brackets at \$2.40 each and $24$ screws at \$0.15 each. What do they cost in all?
cues.working: $6 \times 2.40 = 14.40$ and $24 \times 0.15 = 3.60$, so the total is \$18.00. B adds only the unit prices.

m203-5-3-c.title: Exploded Views and Components, Part 3: Assembly Order and Comparing Costs

cues.prompt: Which part of a garden shed goes on **last**?
cues.working: The floor frame holds the walls, the walls hold the rafters, and the shingles cover the rafters, so the shingles go on last.

m203-6-1.title: Personal Budgets, Part 1: Gross Pay and Net Pay

chapters.title: Gross pay, deductions and net pay

cues.prompt: Sam earns \$17.50 an hour and works $120$ hours in a month. In this example, deductions take $18\%$ of gross pay. What is Sam’s net pay?

m203-6-1-b.title: Personal Budgets, Part 2: Expenses, Surplus and Deficit

cues.prompt: Leah’s net income is \$1,900.00 a month, and her expenses total \$1,985.50. Does Leah’s budget have a surplus or a deficit, and how much?
cues.working: Expenses are more than income, so there is a deficit: $1{,}985.50 - 1{,}900.00 = 85.50$. B has the right amount, but calls it a surplus.

m203-6-1-c.title: Personal Budgets, Part 3: Percent of Income and Circle Graphs

cues.prompt: Noor’s net income is \$1,800 a month, and the phone plan costs \$63 a month. What percent of Noor’s income is the phone plan?
cues.working: $63 \div 1{,}800 = 0.035$, and $0.035 \times 100 = 3.5\%$. C forgets to multiply by $100$, and D divides the wrong way.

m203-6-1-d.title: Personal Budgets, Part 4: Saving for a Goal

cues.prompt: Eli can save \$160 a month toward a \$1,350 laptop. How many months will it take?
cues.working: $1{,}350 \div 160 \approx 8.44$. After $8$ months Eli has only \$1,280, so it takes $9$ months. B rounds down.

cues.prompt: A plan costs \$5.50 a month, includes $15$ transactions, and charges \$0.75 for each extra. Ana makes $23$ transactions in a month. What is Ana’s service charge?
cues.working: Extras: $23 - 15 = 8$, and $8 \times 0.75 = 6.00$. Service charge: $5.50 + 6.00 = 11.50$. B charges for all $23$ transactions, and C leaves out the monthly fee.

m203-6-2-b.title: Banking Services, Part 2: Comparing Plans and the Break-Even Point

cues.prompt: Plan A costs \$2.50 a month, includes $6$ transactions, and charges \$0.75 for each extra. Plan B costs \$8.50 a month with unlimited transactions. What is the break-even point?
cues.working: $8.50 - 2.50 = 6.00$, and $6.00 \div 0.75 = 8$ extra transactions. Add the included ones: $6 + 8 = 14$. B forgets the included transactions.

m203-6-2-c.title: Banking Services, Part 3: Overdrafts and Statements

cues.prompt: A statement shows an opening balance of \$350.00, deposits of \$900.00, and withdrawals of \$1,020.50. What is the closing balance?
cues.working: $350.00 + 900.00 - 1{,}020.50 = 229.50$. B adds the withdrawals instead of subtracting them.

m203-6-2-d.title: Banking Services, Part 4: Reconciling an Account

cues.prompt: A statement balance is \$820.00. A cheque for \$120.00 is outstanding, and a deposit of \$200.00 is not on the statement. What is the adjusted statement balance?
cues.working: $820.00 + 200.00 - 120.00 = 900.00$. B subtracts the deposit and adds the cheque.

m203-7-1.title: Simple and Compound Interest, Part 1: Simple Interest

cues.prompt: Jaxon puts \$1,200 into a GIC that pays $4\%$ simple interest per year. What is it worth after $3$ years?
cues.working: $I = 1{,}200 \times 0.04 \times 3 = 144$, so $A = 1{,}200 + 144 = 1{,}344$. B is only the interest, and C uses $4$ instead of $0.04$.

m203-7-1-b.title: Simple and Compound Interest, Part 2: Time in Months and Missing Values

cues.prompt: A loan of \$2,000 charges $6\%$ simple interest per year. How much interest is charged for $8$ months?
cues.working: $t = \dfrac{8}{12}$ of a year, so $I = 2{,}000 \times 0.06 \times \dfrac{8}{12} = 80$. B uses $t = 8$, and C is the interest for a whole year.

m203-7-1-c.title: Simple and Compound Interest, Part 3: Compound Interest

cues.prompt: \$3,000 earns $6\%$ per year, compounded quarterly. What is it worth after $2$ years?
cues.working: $n = 4$ and $nt = 8$: $A = 3{,}000\left(1 + \dfrac{0.06}{4}\right)^{8} = 3{,}000(1.015)^8 \approx 3{,}379.48$. B is simple interest, and C compounds once a year.

m203-7-1-d.title: Simple and Compound Interest, Part 4: Simple and Compound Compared

cues.prompt: \$2,000 is invested for $15$ years at $5\%$. How much more does it earn compounded annually than with simple interest?
cues.working: Simple: $2{,}000 + 2{,}000 \times 0.05 \times 15 = 3{,}500$. Compound: $2{,}000(1.05)^{15} \approx 4{,}157.86$. The difference is $657.86$. D is the compound amount itself.

m203-7-2.title: The Rule of 72 and Investments, Part 1: The Rule of 72

chapters.title: Rates that do not divide evenly

cues.prompt: An investment earns $9\%$ per year, compounded annually. About how long will it take to double?
cues.working: $72 \div 9 = 8$, so about $8$ years. B divides by $0.09$ instead of $9$.

m203-7-2-b.title: The Rule of 72 and Investments, Part 2: Doubling Again and Again

cues.prompt: \$4,000 earns $3\%$ per year, compounded annually. Use the Rule of 72 to estimate its value in $48$ years.
cues.working: Doubling time: $72 \div 3 = 24$ years, so $48 \div 24 = 2$ doublings: \$4,000 to \$8,000 to \$16,000. B doubles only once.

m203-7-2-c.title: The Rule of 72 and Investments, Part 3: Checking the Rule and Comparing Offers

cues.prompt: For \$8,000 over $10$ years, Offer A pays $5.5\%$ simple interest and Offer B pays $5\%$ compounded quarterly. Which is better, and by how much?

m203-7-3.title: Credit Cards and Loans, Part 1: Credit Card Interest

cues.prompt: A card charges $18.99\%$ per year, charged daily. How much interest is charged on an unpaid balance of \$600 for $31$ days?
cues.working: $600 \times 0.1899 \div 365 \times 31 \approx 9.68$. B uses $18.99$ instead of $0.1899$, and C is the interest for a whole year.

m203-7-3-b.title: Credit Cards and Loans, Part 2: The New Balance and the Minimum Payment

cues.prompt: A statement balance is \$900.00, and \$300.00 is paid. Interest is charged on the unpaid amount at $19.99\%$ per year for $30$ days, and there are \$75.50 in new purchases. What is the new balance?
cues.working: Unpaid: $900 - 300 = 600$. Interest: $600 \times 0.1999 \div 365 \times 30 \approx 9.86$. New balance: $600 + 9.86 + 75.50 = 685.36$. B charges interest on the whole \$900, and C leaves out the new purchases.

m203-7-3-c.title: Credit Cards and Loans, Part 3: The Cost of Carrying a Balance

cues.prompt: You expect to carry an average balance of \$1,000 for a year. Card A charges $21.99\%$ with no fee. Card B charges $11.99\%$ with a \$79 annual fee. Which costs less, and by how much?
cues.working: Card A: $1{,}000 \times 0.2199 = 219.90$. Card B: $1{,}000 \times 0.1199 + 79 = 198.90$. Card B costs \$21.00 less. C forgets the fee.

m203-7-3-d.title: Credit Cards and Loans, Part 4: The Cost of a Loan

cues.prompt: A car loan of \$15,000 has payments of \$295.50 a month for $5$ years. What is the finance charge?
cues.working: $5 \times 12 = 60$ payments, and $295.50 \times 60 = 17{,}730.00$. Finance charge: $17{,}730.00 - 15{,}000 = 2{,}730.00$. B is the total paid.

m203-7-3-e.title: Credit Cards and Loans, Part 5: Comparing Credit Options

cues.prompt: A laptop has a cash price of \$649.99, or $52$ weekly rent-to-own payments of \$21.99. What is the finance charge?
cues.working: $21.99 \times 52 = 1{,}143.48$, and $1{,}143.48 - 649.99 = 493.49$. B is the total of the payments, and C adds the cash price instead of subtracting it.

m203-8-1.title: Bar Graphs, Histograms and Circle Graphs, Part 1: Bar Graphs

cues.prompt: On a bar graph of seed sales, the grid lines go up by $50$. The Canola bar stops halfway between $300$ and $350$, and the Barley bar stops on $200$. How many more bags of canola than barley were sold?
cues.working: Halfway between $300$ and $350$ is $325$, and $325 - 200 = 125$. B reads the Canola bar as $350$, and C reads it as $300$.

m203-8-1-b.title: Bar Graphs, Histograms and Circle Graphs, Part 2: Circle Graphs

chapters.title: From a percent to an amount

cues.prompt: A circle graph shows how $600$ students get to school, and the Bus sector is $30\%$. How many students take the bus, and what is the angle of the Bus sector?
cues.working: $0.30 \times 600 = 180$ students, and $0.30 \times 360 = 108^\circ$. B uses the percent as the angle.

m203-8-1-c.title: Bar Graphs, Histograms and Circle Graphs, Part 3: From Counts to a Circle Graph

cues.prompt: A farm supply store sold $120$ bags of seed, and $45$ were canola. What angle would the Canola sector have on a circle graph?
cues.working: $\dfrac{45}{120} = 0.375$, and $0.375 \times 360 = 135^\circ$. B is the percent, not the angle, and D is the angle for the other bags.

m203-8-1-d.title: Bar Graphs, Histograms and Circle Graphs, Part 4: Histograms

cues.prompt: Ages: $18,\ 25,\ 20,\ 31,\ 29,\ 40,\ 22,\ 19,\ 35,\ 20$. What is the frequency of the $20$–$29$ interval?
cues.working: The ages from $20$ to $29$ are $20,\ 20,\ 22,\ 25,\ 29$, so the frequency is $5$. B leaves out the two $20$s on the boundary.

m203-8-1-e.title: Bar Graphs, Histograms and Circle Graphs, Part 5: Using a Histogram

cues.prompt: What percent of these customers were $50$ or older, to the nearest tenth of a percent?
cues.working: $6 + 2 = 8$ customers, and $\dfrac{8}{42} \times 100 \approx 19.0\%$. B gives the count, not the percent, and C is the percent aged $40$ or older.

m203-8-2.title: Line Graphs and Choosing a Graph, Part 1: Reading a Line Graph

cues.prompt: The table gives the points of a line graph of the water in a dugout. Which describes the trend?
choices: down from May to August, then up in September
up from May to August, then down
about the same the whole time
cues.working: The depth falls from $240$ to $150$ cm by August, then rises to $160$ cm in September. B misses the change of direction.

m203-8-2-b.title: Line Graphs and Choosing a Graph, Part 2: Rate of Change on a Line Graph

chapters.title: How fast did it warm up?

cues.prompt: On a line graph, the water in a dugout is $240$ cm deep on June 1 and $180$ cm deep on August 1. What is the average rate of change?
cues.working: Change in depth: $180 - 240 = -60$ cm, over $2$ months, so $-60 \div 2 = -30$ cm per month. B forgets to divide by the time.

m203-8-2-c.title: Line Graphs and Choosing a Graph, Part 3: Predicting from a Steady Trend

cues.prompt: In this example, a line graph shows a calf’s mass rising steadily from $250$ kg, by $1.2$ kg a day. If the trend continues, what will its mass be after $30$ days?
cues.working: $30 \times 1.2 = 36$ kg gained, and $250 + 36 = 286$ kg. B adds $30$ instead of $30 \times 1.2$, and C is only the gain.

m203-8-2-d.title: Line Graphs and Choosing a Graph, Part 4: Choosing the Best Graph

cues.prompt: Ty recorded the depth of the water in a dugout on the first day of every month for a year. Which graph best shows how the depth changed?
cues.working: The depth changes over time, so a line graph is best. A circle graph is for parts of one whole.

m203-8-2-e.title: Line Graphs and Choosing a Graph, Part 5: Misleading Graphs

cues.prompt: A bar graph’s vertical axis starts at $200$. Its bars show $210$ and $230$, so the second bar looks $3$ times as tall. What was the real percent increase?
cues.working: $230 - 210 = 20$, and $\dfrac{20}{210} \times 100 \approx 9.5\%$. B trusts the cut-off bars, and D is the increase, not a percent.

m203-8-3.title: Numerical Puzzles and Games, Part 1: Number Patterns

cues.prompt: Triangles in a row are made of toothpicks. Figure $1$ uses $3$ toothpicks, figure $2$ uses $5$ and figure $3$ uses $7$. How many does figure $15$ use?
cues.working: Each figure adds $2$. From figure $1$ to figure $15$ there are $14$ steps: $3 + 14 \times 2 = 31$. B counts $15$ separate triangles.

m203-8-3-b.title: Numerical Puzzles and Games, Part 2: Magic Squares

cues.prompt: A $3$ by $3$ magic square has a top row of $10,\ 3,\ 8$. Its left column is $10,\ 5$ and a missing number. What is the missing number?
cues.working: The magic sum is $10 + 3 + 8 = 21$, so the missing number is $21 - (10 + 5) = 6$. C is the centre number, $21 \div 3$.

m203-8-3-c.title: Numerical Puzzles and Games, Part 3: Cage Puzzles and Logic Puzzles

cues.prompt: I am a two-digit number. My digits add up to $9$. I am a multiple of $4$. My tens digit is less than my ones digit. What number am I?
cues.working: Digits adding to $9$: $18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72, 81, 90$. Multiples of $4$: $36$ and $72$. Tens digit less than ones digit: $36$. B breaks the last clue.

m203-8-3-d.title: Numerical Puzzles and Games, Part 4: Winning Strategies

chapters.title: Grabbing as many as you can

cues.prompt: Players take $1$, $2$ or $3$ counters, and whoever takes the last counter wins. There are $15$ counters, and it is your turn. How many should you take?
cues.working: Leave a multiple of $4$: $15 - 3 = 12$. Taking $1$ leaves $14$, and taking $2$ leaves $13$, neither a multiple of $4$.

m204-1-1.title: Integers and the Order of Operations, Part 1: Working with Integers

cues.prompt: The temperature drops $2$ degrees every hour for $6$ hours. What is the total change?
cues.working: A drop of $2$ is $-2$, and $6 \times (-2) = -12$. B forgets that a drop is negative.

m204-1-1-b.title: Integers and the Order of Operations, Part 2: The Order of Operations

cues.prompt: Calculate $6 + (-12) \div 3$.
cues.working: Divide first: $(-12) \div 3 = -4$. Then add: $6 + (-4) = 2$. B adds first, working left to right.

m204-1-1-c.title: Integers and the Order of Operations, Part 3: Integers at Work and at Home

cues.prompt: The overnight lows for four nights were $-4$, $-9$, $3$ and $-6$ degrees. What is the mean low?
cues.working: Total: $-4 + (-9) + 3 + (-6) = -16$. Mean: $-16 \div 4 = -4$. C treats the $3$ as $-3$, and D forgets to divide.

m204-1-2.title: Fractions and Mixed Numbers, Part 1: Mixed Numbers and Improper Fractions

cues.prompt: Write $3\tfrac58$ as an improper fraction.
cues.working: $3 \times 8 = 24$, and $24 + 5 = 29$, so $3\tfrac58 = \tfrac{29}{8}$. B adds $3$ and $5$, and C forgets to add the $5$.

m204-1-2-b.title: Fractions and Mixed Numbers, Part 2: Adding and Subtracting

cues.prompt: A pipe is $4\tfrac38$ feet long. You cut off $1\tfrac34$ feet. How much is left?
cues.working: $4\tfrac38 = \tfrac{35}{8}$ and $1\tfrac34 = \tfrac{14}{8}$, so $\tfrac{35}{8} - \tfrac{14}{8} = \tfrac{21}{8} = 2\tfrac58$. C adds instead of subtracting.

m204-1-2-c.title: Fractions and Mixed Numbers, Part 3: Multiplying

cues.prompt: A recipe uses $1\tfrac13$ cups of sugar. How much sugar do $3$ batches need?
cues.working: $1\tfrac13 = \tfrac43$, and $3 \times \tfrac43 = \tfrac{12}{3} = 4$. B multiplies only the whole number.

m204-1-2-d.title: Fractions and Mixed Numbers, Part 4: Two-Step Problems

cues.prompt: A roll has $20$ feet of ribbon. You cut $4$ pieces, each $3\tfrac12$ feet long. How much ribbon is left?
cues.working: $4 \times 3\tfrac12 = 4 \times \tfrac72 = 14$ feet, and $20 - 14 = 6$ feet. B subtracts only one piece, and C is the ribbon used.

m204-1-3.title: Ratios, Rates and Proportions, Part 1: Ratios

cues.prompt: A crew has $15$ carpenters and $10$ labourers. What is the ratio of labourers to carpenters, in simplest form?
cues.working: Labourers first: $10 : 15$. Both divide by $5$: $2 : 3$. B has the terms in the wrong order, and C is not in simplest form.

m204-1-3-b.title: Ratios, Rates and Proportions, Part 2: Rates and Unit Rates

cues.prompt: A $4$ L jug of milk costs \$6.20. What is the price per litre?
cues.working: Divide the price by the litres: $6.20 \div 4 = 1.55$. B multiplies, and C divides the litres by the price.

m204-1-3-c.title: Ratios, Rates and Proportions, Part 3: Proportions

cues.prompt: A recipe uses $3$ cups of flour for $24$ cookies. How much flour is needed for $40$ cookies?
cues.working: For one cookie: $3 \div 24 = \tfrac18$ cup. For $40$: $40 \times \tfrac18 = 5$ cups. B adds $16$ instead of multiplying.

m204-1-3-d.title: Ratios, Rates and Proportions, Part 4: Sharing a Total in a Ratio

cues.prompt: Trail mix is nuts, raisins and chocolate in the ratio $4 : 3 : 1$. How much chocolate is in $640$ g of trail mix?
cues.working: $4 + 3 + 1 = 8$ parts, and $640 \div 8 = 80$ g in one part. Chocolate is $1$ part: $80$ g. C is the raisins.

m204-1-4.title: Percent Problems, Part 1: Percent of a Number

cues.prompt: What is a $15\%$ tip on a \$60 meal?
cues.working: $10\%$ of \$60 is \$6, and $5\%$ is \$3, so $15\%$ is \$9. B is only $10\%$, and D is the meal plus the tip.

cues.prompt: A hockey team won $14$ of its $20$ games. What percent of its games did it win?
cues.working: $14 \div 20 = 0.7$, and $0.7 \times 100 = 70\%$. B divides the wrong way, and D is the percent it did not win.

m204-1-4-c.title: Percent Problems, Part 3: Percent Increase and Decrease

cues.prompt: The price of gas drops from \$1.50 to \$1.20 per litre. What is the percent decrease?
cues.working: Change: $1.50 - 1.20 = 0.30$. Divide by the original: $0.30 \div 1.50 = 0.2$, which is $20\%$. B divides by the new price.

m204-1-4-d.title: Percent Problems, Part 4: New Amounts and Finding the Whole

cues.prompt: A \$70 deposit is $20\%$ of the full price of a bike. What is the full price?
cues.working: $70 \div 0.20 = 350$. Check: $20\%$ of \$350 is \$70. B multiplies instead of dividing, and D is what is still owed.

m204-2-1.title: Unit Price and the Best Buy, Part 1: What Is a Unit Price?

cues.prompt: A pack of $12$ pencils costs \$3.60. What is the unit price?
cues.working: Money first: $3.60 \div 12 = 0.30$. B divides the wrong way, and C multiplies.

m204-2-1-b.title: Unit Price and the Best Buy, Part 2: Different Sizes and Units

cues.prompt: A $400$ g jar of peanut butter costs \$3.20. What is the price per $100$ g?
cues.working: $400 \div 100 = 4$ groups, and $3.20 \div 4 = 0.80$. B divides by $400$ instead of $4$, and C divides the wrong way.

m204-2-1-c.title: Unit Price and the Best Buy, Part 3: Finding the Best Buy

cues.prompt: Laundry soap costs \$7.50 for $2$ L or \$17.50 for $5$ L. Which is the best buy?
choices: the $5$ L jug, at \$3.50 per litre
the $2$ L jug, at \$3.75 per litre
They cost the same per litre.
the $5$ L jug, at \$17.50 per litre
cues.working: $7.50 \div 2 = 3.75$ and $17.50 \div 5 = 3.50$, so the $5$ L jug costs less per litre.

m204-2-1-d.title: Unit Price and the Best Buy, Part 4: Deals, Coupons and Common Sense

cues.prompt: Granola bars: a box of $6$ for \$3.00, with a coupon for \$0.60 off, or a box of $10$ for \$4.50. Which is the better buy per bar?
choices: the box of $6$ with the coupon, at \$0.40 per bar
the box of $10$, at \$0.45 per bar
the box of $6$, at \$0.50 per bar
They cost the same per bar.
cues.working: With the coupon: $3.00 - 0.60 = 2.40$, and $2.40 \div 6 = 0.40$. Box of $10$: $4.50 \div 10 = 0.45$. C forgets the coupon.

m204-2-2.title: Sales, Discounts and Taxes, Part 1: Discounts and Sale Prices

cues.prompt: A drill is regularly \$120. It is $15\%$ off. What is the sale price?
cues.working: Discount: $0.15 \times 120 = 18$. Sale price: $120 - 18 = 102$. B is the discount, and C takes off \$15 instead of $15\%$.

m204-2-2-b.title: Sales, Discounts and Taxes, Part 2: Two Deals at Once

cues.prompt: A jacket is regularly \$80. It is $25\%$ off, then another $10\%$ off at the till. What is the final price?
cues.working: After $25\%$ off: $0.75 \times 80 = 60$. After another $10\%$ off: $0.9 \times 60 = 54$. B adds the discounts to make $35\%$, and C forgets the second discount.

m204-2-2-c.title: Sales, Discounts and Taxes, Part 3: Subtotal, GST and Total

cues.prompt: A subtotal is \$24.60. In this example, GST is $5\%$. What is the total?
cues.working: GST: $0.05 \times 24.60 = 1.23$. Total: $24.60 + 1.23 = 25.83$. B is only the GST, and D adds \$5 instead of $5\%$.

m204-2-2-d.title: Sales, Discounts and Taxes, Part 4: Paying, Change and Comparing Stores

cues.prompt: Your total is \$17.35. You pay with a \$20 bill. How much change should you get?

m204-2-3.title: Paying Over Time, Part 1: Instalment Plans and the Finance Charge

cues.prompt: A stereo costs \$340 cash. The plan is \$50 down and $10$ monthly payments of \$32. What is the finance charge?
cues.working: Total cost: $50 + 10 \times 32 = 370$. Finance charge: $370 - 340 = 30$. B is the total cost of the plan.

m204-2-3-b.title: Paying Over Time, Part 2: No Money Down and Weekly Payments

cues.prompt: A phone costs \$999 cash, or \$0 down and $36$ monthly payments of \$35. What is the finance charge?
cues.working: Total cost: $36 \times 35 = 1{,}260$. Finance charge: $1{,}260 - 999 = 261$. B is the total cost of the plan.

m204-2-3-c.title: Paying Over Time, Part 3: Comparing Payment Plans

cues.prompt: A fridge costs \$1,200 cash. The plan is $10\%$ down, then $18$ monthly payments of \$66. What is the total cost of the plan?
cues.working: Down: $0.1 \times 1{,}200 = 120$. Payments: $18 \times 66 = 1{,}188$. Total: $120 + 1{,}188 = 1{,}308$. B forgets the down payment, and D is the finance charge.

m204-3-1.title: Wages and Overtime, Part 1: Gross Pay from an Hourly Wage

cues.prompt: Nadia earns \$15.00 per hour on weekdays and \$18.00 per hour on weekends. This week Nadia worked $20$ weekday hours and $6$ weekend hours. What is the gross pay?
cues.working: Weekdays: $20 \times 15.00 = 300.00$. Weekends: $6 \times 18.00 = 108.00$. Gross pay: $300.00 + 108.00 = 408.00$. B pays every hour at the weekday rate, and C at the weekend rate.

m204-3-1-b.title: Wages and Overtime, Part 2: Reading a Timecard

cues.prompt: A shift runs from 8:00 a.m. to 2:45 p.m., with a 30-minute unpaid break. How many paid hours is that?
cues.working: 8:00 a.m. to noon is $4$ h, noon to 2:00 p.m. is $2$ h, then $45$ min: $6.75$ h. Take away the break: $6.75 - 0.5 = 6.25$ h. B forgets the break, and C treats minutes as decimals.

m204-3-1-c.title: Wages and Overtime, Part 3: Overtime Pay

cues.prompt: Theo earns \$20.00 per hour. Hours over $8$ in a day are paid at time-and-a-half. On Friday Theo worked $10$ hours. What is the gross pay for the day?
cues.working: Regular: $8 \times 20.00 = 160.00$. Overtime: $2 \times 30.00 = 60.00$. Gross pay: $160.00 + 60.00 = 220.00$. B pays every hour at time-and-a-half, C forgets overtime, and D uses double time.

m204-3-1-d.title: Wages and Overtime, Part 4: Overtime Day by Day

cues.prompt: Ava earns \$16.00 per hour. Hours over $8$ in a day are paid at time-and-a-half. Ava worked $10$ hours on Monday, $6$ on Tuesday and $9$ on Wednesday. What is the gross pay?
cues.working: Overtime: $2 + 1 = 3$ h at $1.5 \times 16.00 = 24.00$, so $72.00$. Regular: $8 + 6 + 8 = 22$ h, so $22 \times 16.00 = 352.00$. Gross pay: $352.00 + 72.00 = 424.00$. B forgets overtime, and C uses double time.

m204-3-2.title: Other Ways to Earn, Part 1: Salary

chapters.title: Two weeks or twice a month?

cues.prompt: Diego earns a salary of \$45,600 a year, paid monthly. How much is each pay?
cues.working: Monthly means $12$ pays: $45{,}600 \div 12 = 3{,}800.00$. B divides by $24$, C by $26$, and D by $52$.

m204-3-2-b.title: Other Ways to Earn, Part 2: Commission

cues.prompt: Jasmine earns \$250 a week plus $4\%$ of sales. This week Jasmine sold \$7,200 worth of phones. What is the pay for the week?
cues.working: Commission: $0.04 \times 7{,}200 = 288.00$. Total: $250.00 + 288.00 = 538.00$. B forgets the base, C uses $0.004$, and D adds the base to the sales.

m204-3-2-c.title: Other Ways to Earn, Part 3: Piecework

cues.prompt: A berry picker earns \$0.75 per basket. In a $6$-hour shift, the picker fills $96$ baskets. What is the pay per hour?
cues.working: Pay: $0.75 \times 96 = 72.00$. Per hour: $72.00 \div 6 = 12.00$. B is the pay for the shift, and C is the baskets per hour.

m204-3-2-d.title: Other Ways to Earn, Part 4: Sharing Tips

cues.prompt: Zoe, Raj and Lena share \$270 in tips by hours worked. Zoe worked $5$ hours, Raj $4$ hours and Lena $6$ hours. How much does Lena get?
cues.working: Total hours: $5 + 4 + 6 = 15$. Per hour: $270 \div 15 = 18.00$. Lena: $6 \times 18.00 = 108.00$. B shares equally, C is the tips per hour, and D is Raj’s share.

m204-3-3.title: Deductions and Net Pay, Part 1: Reading a Pay Stub

chapters.title: Net pay from a pay stub

cues.prompt: A pay stub shows gross pay of \$960.00. The deductions are CPP \$48.00, EI \$16.00, income tax \$96.00 and union dues \$12.00. What is the net pay?
cues.working: Total deductions: $48 + 16 + 96 + 12 = 172$. Net pay: $960.00 - 172.00 = 788.00$. B takes off only the income tax, and C is the total deductions.

m204-3-3-b.title: Deductions and Net Pay, Part 2: Deductions from Percents

cues.prompt: Gross pay is \$850.00. Suppose $5\%$ is taken for CPP, $2\%$ for EI and $10\%$ for income tax. What is the net pay?
cues.working: CPP: $42.50$. EI: $17.00$. Income tax: $85.00$. Total: $144.50$. Net pay: $850.00 - 144.50 = 705.50$. B is the total deductions, C takes off only EI, and D adds the deductions.

m204-3-3-c.title: Deductions and Net Pay, Part 3: From Hours to Net Pay

cues.prompt: Sam works $30$ hours at \$18.00 per hour. Suppose $5\%$ is taken for CPP, $2\%$ for EI and $10\%$ for income tax, and union dues are \$10.00. What is the net pay?
cues.working: Gross pay: $30 \times 18.00 = 540.00$. Deductions: $27.00 + 10.80 + 54.00 + 10.00 = 101.80$. Net pay: $540.00 - 101.80 = 438.20$. B forgets the union dues, C is the total deductions, and D takes the percents off the hourly wage.

m204-4-1.title: Making a Budget, Part 1: Income and Expenses

cues.prompt: Tomas takes home \$1,850 a month. His expenses are rent \$820, phone \$60, bus pass \$110, groceries \$350 and entertainment \$90. How much is left over each month?
cues.working: Expenses: $820 + 60 + 110 + 350 + 90 = 1{,}430$. Left over: $1{,}850 - 1{,}430 = 420$. B is the total expenses, and C forgets the entertainment.

m204-4-1-b.title: Making a Budget, Part 2: Fixed and Variable Expenses

cues.prompt: Which list has only **variable** expenses?
choices: groceries, gas for a car, eating out
phone plan, bus pass, car insurance
rent, gas for a car, phone plan
cues.working: Groceries, gas and eating out change from month to month. Rent, a phone plan, a bus pass and car insurance are fixed. C is a list of fixed expenses only.

m204-4-1-c.title: Making a Budget, Part 3: Budgets as Percents

cues.prompt: Lena takes home \$2,500 a month and pays \$900 for rent. What percent of the take-home pay goes to rent?
cues.working: $900 \div 2{,}500 \times 100 = 36\%$. B divides the wrong way, C forgets to multiply by $100$, and D is the percent that is left.

m204-4-1-d.title: Making a Budget, Part 4: Saving for a Goal

chapters.title: Costs that do not come every month

cues.prompt: Kiara wants \$1,200 for a damage deposit in $8$ months. Right now Kiara has \$90 left over each month. How much less must Kiara spend each month?
cues.working: Save each month: $1{,}200 \div 8 = 150$. Short by $150 - 90 = 60$. B is the monthly savings, and D subtracts the \$90 from the whole goal.

m204-4-2.title: Simple Interest, Part 1: What Is Interest?

cues.prompt: Felix puts \$1,500 in a savings account that pays $4\%$ per year simple interest. How much interest does it earn in $2$ years?
cues.working: One year: $1{,}500 \times 0.04 = 60$. Two years: $60 \times 2 = 120$. B is one year only, C is the total in the account, and D uses $4$ instead of $0.04$.

m204-4-2-b.title: Simple Interest, Part 2: The Formula I = Prt

cues.prompt: A loan of \$1,800 charges $5\%$ per year simple interest. How much interest is charged in $4$ years?
cues.working: $I = 1{,}800 \times 0.05 \times 4 = 360$. B is one year only, C uses $r = 5$, and D is the principal plus the interest.

m204-4-2-c.title: Simple Interest, Part 3: Months and the Total Amount

cues.prompt: A loan of \$2,400 is for $9$ months at $6\%$ per year simple interest. What is the total to pay back?
cues.working: $t = 9 \div 12 = 0.75$. $I = 2{,}400 \times 0.06 \times 0.75 = 108$. $A = 2{,}400 + 108 = 2{,}508$. B is the interest only, C uses $t = 9$, and D uses a whole year.

m204-4-2-d.title: Simple Interest, Part 4: Finding the Rate or the Time

cues.prompt: A loan of \$1,200 at $4\%$ per year simple interest cost \$72 in interest. How many months was the loan?
cues.working: $72 = 1{,}200 \times 0.04 \times t = 48t$, so $t = 72 \div 48 = 1.5$ years, which is $1.5 \times 12 = 18$ months. B forgets to change years to months.

m204-4-3.title: Credit Cards and Loans, Part 1: How a Credit Card Bill Works

cues.prompt: An unpaid balance is \$650. The card charges $1.5\%$ per month on the unpaid balance. How much interest is charged this month?
cues.working: $1.5\% = 0.015$, and $650 \times 0.015 = 9.75$. B uses $0.15$, C uses $1.5$, and D is the new balance.

m204-4-3-b.title: Credit Cards and Loans, Part 2: Yearly Rates and Monthly Interest

chapters.title: One month from a yearly rate

cues.prompt: An unpaid balance is \$2,400. The card charges $18\%$ per year. What is the interest for one month?
cues.working: $2{,}400 \times 0.18 \div 12 = 36.00$. B is the interest for a whole year, and D is the new balance.

m204-4-3-c.title: Credit Cards and Loans, Part 3: The Cost of a Loan

chapters.title: A loan for a used car

cues.prompt: Ivy borrows \$6,000 and pays it back with $36$ monthly payments of \$189.50. What is the cost of borrowing?
cues.working: Total paid: $189.50 \times 36 = 6{,}822$. Cost of borrowing: $6{,}822 - 6{,}000 = 822$. B is the total paid.

m204-4-3-d.title: Credit Cards and Loans, Part 4: Why Paying the Full Balance Matters

cues.prompt: A statement balance is \$1,200. The card charges $2\%$ per month on the unpaid balance. If you pay \$400, how much interest is charged next month?
cues.working: Unpaid: $1{,}200 - 400 = 800$. Interest: $800 \times 0.02 = 16.00$. B uses the whole balance, and C uses the amount paid.

m204-4-4.title: Cars and Homes, Part 1: The Monthly Cost of a Vehicle

chapters.title: The real cost of a car

cues.prompt: A car payment is \$310 a month. Insurance is \$1,920 a year, gas is \$140 a month and maintenance is \$45 a month. What is the total monthly cost?
cues.working: Insurance: $1{,}920 \div 12 = 160$. Total: $310 + 160 + 140 + 45 = 655$. B forgets the insurance, C adds the yearly insurance, and D is only the payment.

m204-4-4-b.title: Cars and Homes, Part 2: Fuel Costs

chapters.title: A car or a pickup truck?

cues.prompt: A car uses $7.5$ L/100 km and drives $1200$ km a month. Gas costs \$1.60 per litre. What is the monthly gas cost?
cues.working: Litres: $1200 \div 100 \times 7.5 = 12 \times 7.5 = 90$ L. Cost: $90 \times 1.60 = 144.00$. B forgets to divide by $100$, and C is the litres, not the dollars.

m204-4-4-c.title: Cars and Homes, Part 3: Renting a Home

cues.prompt: Three roommates share an apartment. Rent is \$1,350, utilities are \$180 and internet is \$60 a month. They split the costs equally. What does each person pay?
cues.working: Total: $1{,}350 + 180 + 60 = 1{,}590$. Each: $1{,}590 \div 3 = 530$. B is the total, C splits it two ways, and D shares only the rent.

m204-4-4-d.title: Cars and Homes, Part 4: How Much Rent Can You Afford?

cues.prompt: Ravi takes home \$3,100 a month. Using the $30\%$ guideline, what is the most rent Ravi should pay?
cues.working: $0.3 \times 3{,}100 = 930$. B is the $70\%$ that is left, C is only $10\%$, and D divides by $3$.

m204-5-1.title: Using Formulas, Part 1: Substituting into a Formula

cues.prompt: Use $E = rh$. Malik earns \$17.25 per hour and works $8$ hours. What is the pay?
cues.working: $E = 17.25 \times 8 = 138.00$. B adds instead of multiplying, and D works ten hours.

m204-5-1-b.title: Using Formulas, Part 2: Formulas with More Than One Step

cues.prompt: A taxi charges $C = 3.5 + 2d$, where $C$ is in dollars and $d$ is in kilometres. What is the fare for a $9$ km ride?
cues.working: $C = 3.5 + 2 \times 9 = 3.5 + 18 = 21.5$. B adds first, and D forgets the starting fee.

m204-5-1-c.title: Using Formulas, Part 3: The Temperature Formula

cues.prompt: Use $F = 1.8C + 32$. What is $-10^\circ\text{C}$ in degrees Fahrenheit?
cues.working: $F = 1.8 \times (-10) + 32 = -18 + 32 = 14$. B uses $+10$, and D forgets to add $32$.

m204-5-1-d.title: Using Formulas, Part 4: Formulas in Two-Step Jobs

cues.prompt: A room is $5.2$ m long and $3.5$ m wide. Carpet costs \$32.00 per square metre. What will the carpet cost?
cues.working: Area: $5.2 \times 3.5 = 18.2\ \text{m}^2$. Cost: $18.2 \times 32.00 = 582.40$. B uses the perimeter, $17.4$ m, and C is the area, not the cost.

cues.prompt: Solve $y - 9 = 14$.
cues.working: To undo $-\ 9$, add $9$ to both sides: $y = 14 + 9 = 23$. Check: $23 - 9 = 14$. B subtracts instead of adding.

cues.prompt: Solve $4x - 3 = 25$.
cues.working: Add $3$ to both sides: $4x = 28$. Divide by $4$: $x = 7$. Check: $4 \times 7 - 3 = 25$. B subtracts $3$ instead of adding, and D divides first.

m204-5-2-c.title: Solving Equations, Part 3: Using a Formula Backwards

chapters.title: How far was the taxi ride?

cues.prompt: Use $E = rh$. Jada earned \$504.00 at \$16.80 per hour. How many hours did Jada work?
cues.working: $504.00 = 16.80h$, so $h = 504.00 \div 16.80 = 30$. B multiplies instead of dividing, and C subtracts.

m204-5-2-d.title: Solving Equations, Part 4: Checking Your Answer

cues.prompt: Ella solved $5p - 12 = 33$ and got $p = 4.2$. Check the answer. What is the correct solution?
cues.working: Check: $5 \times 4.2 - 12 = 9$, not $33$. Add $12$: $5p = 45$, so $p = 9$. Check: $5 \times 9 - 12 = 33$. B subtracted $12$ instead of adding it, and C forgets the $12$.

m204-5-3.title: Tables and Graphs, Part 1: Tables of Values

cues.prompt: The rule is $P = 16h$. What are the pay values for $1$, $2$, $3$ and $4$ hours?
cues.working: $16 \times 1 = 16$, $16 \times 2 = 32$, $16 \times 3 = 48$, $16 \times 4 = 64$. Each hour adds $16$. B adds $1$ each time, and C adds the hours to $16$.

m204-5-3-b.title: Tables and Graphs, Part 2: Reading a Graph

cues.prompt: On the graph of $P = 15h$, you start at $105$ on the pay axis, go across to the line, then down. Which number of hours do you land on?
cues.working: $105 \div 15 = 7$, so the point is $(7,\ 105)$. Check: $15 \times 7 = 105$. C multiplies instead of dividing.

m204-5-3-c.title: Tables and Graphs, Part 3: Rules with a Start Value

cues.prompt: A taxi charges $C = 5 + 3d$, where $C$ is in dollars and $d$ is in kilometres. What is the fare for $4$ km?
cues.working: $C = 5 + 3 \times 4 = 5 + 12 = 17$. B forgets the start value, C adds first, and D is only the start value.

m204-5-3-d.title: Tables and Graphs, Part 4: Matching a Rule to a Graph

cues.prompt: A line meets the vertical axis at $30$ and goes up $10$ for each hour to the right. Which rule does it show?
cues.working: The start value is $30$ and the rate is $10$ per hour, so $C = 30 + 10h$. B swaps the start value and the rate.

cues.prompt: A jug holds $3500$ mL of juice. How many litres is that?
cues.working: $1$ L $= 1000$ mL. Litres are bigger, so divide: $3500 \div 1000 = 3.5$ L. B multiplies, and C and D divide by $100$ and $10$.

cues.prompt: A roll of fabric is $4$ yd long. How many feet is that?
cues.working: $1$ yd $= 3$ ft. Feet are smaller, so multiply: $4 \times 3 = 12$ ft. B uses $12$, C divides, and D uses $100$.

chapters.title: A window in feet and inches

cues.prompt: A baby weighs $7$ lb $6$ oz. What is the weight in ounces?
cues.working: $7 \times 16 = 112$ oz, and $112 + 6 = 118$ oz. B uses $10$ instead of $16$, and C uses $12$.

m204-6-2.title: SI and Imperial, Part 1: Conversion Factors

chapters.title: A ruler from the United States

cues.prompt: A tablet screen is $10$ in across. Use $1$ in $= 2.54$ cm. How many centimetres is that?
cues.working: $10 \times 2.54 = 25.4$ cm. Estimate: $10 \times 2.5 = 25$. B divides, and D adds.

m204-6-2-b.title: SI and Imperial, Part 2: Multiply or Divide?

cues.prompt: A suitcase weighs $44$ lb. Use $1$ kg $\approx 2.2$ lb. What is its mass in kilograms?
cues.working: A kilogram is bigger, so divide: $44 \div 2.2 = 20$ kg. B multiplies, and C and D subtract or add.

m204-6-2-c.title: SI and Imperial, Part 3: Speeds and Heights

chapters.title: A speed in miles per hour

cues.prompt: A basketball player is $6$ ft $1$ in tall. Use $1$ in $= 2.54$ cm. What is the height in centimetres, to the nearest tenth?
cues.working: Step 1: $6 \times 12 + 1 = 73$ in. Step 2: $73 \times 2.54 = 185.42 \approx 185.4$ cm. B uses $6.1$ ft as $61$ in, and C divides.

m204-6-2-d.title: SI and Imperial, Part 4: Filling a Gas Tank

cues.prompt: A car has a $15$-gallon (US) tank. Gas costs \$1.60 per litre. Use $1$ US gallon $\approx 3.79$ L. What does it cost to fill the empty tank?
cues.working: Litres: $15 \times 3.79 = 56.85$ L. Cost: $56.85 \times 1.60 = 90.96$. B forgets to convert, and C rounds to $57$ L too early.

cues.prompt: Which temperature makes sense for the inside of a fridge?
cues.working: A fridge is cold but above freezing: just above $0^\circ$C. $4^\circ$F is below freezing, $40^\circ$C is hotter than your body, and $75^\circ$F is warmer than a room.

cues.prompt: Use $F = 1.8C + 32$. What is $15^\circ$C in degrees Fahrenheit?
cues.working: $1.8 \times 15 = 27$, and $27 + 32 = 59$. B adds first, C forgets to add $32$, and D adds $32$ to $15$ without multiplying.

cues.prompt: Use $C = (F - 32) \div 1.8$. What is $104^\circ$F in degrees Celsius?
cues.working: $104 - 32 = 72$, and $72 \div 1.8 = 40$. B divides first, C multiplies by $1.8$, and D forgets to divide.

m204-7-1.title: Perimeter, Part 1: Perimeter of a Rectangle

cues.prompt: A rectangular patio is $12$ m long and $7.5$ m wide. What is its perimeter?
cues.working: $P = 2 \times (12 + 7.5) = 2 \times 19.5 = 39$ m. B adds only two sides, and C multiplies, which gives the area.

m204-7-1-b.title: Perimeter, Part 2: Other Shapes with Straight Sides

cues.prompt: A deck is a regular octagon. An octagon has $8$ sides. Each side is $1.2$ m. What is the perimeter?
cues.working: $8 \times 1.2 = 9.6$ m. B uses $6$ sides, C uses $4$, and D adds $8 + 1.2$.

m204-7-1-c.title: Perimeter, Part 3: Circumference of a Circle

cues.prompt: A bike wheel has a radius of $0.35$ m. What is its circumference, to the nearest tenth of a metre?
cues.working: $d = 2 \times 0.35 = 0.7$ m. $C = \pi \times 0.7 \approx 2.20$ m. B uses the radius, and C is the diameter.

m204-7-1-d.title: Perimeter, Part 4: The Cost of Edging and Fencing

cues.prompt: A rectangular yard is $10$ m by $7$ m. Fencing costs \$12.50 per metre. What will the fencing cost?
cues.working: Perimeter: $10 + 7 + 10 + 7 = 34$ m. Cost: $34 \times 12.50 = 425.00$. B uses the area, $70$ m², C uses only two sides, and D is the perimeter, not the cost.

m204-7-2.title: Area, Part 1: Area of a Rectangle

cues.prompt: A rectangular lawn is $5.5$ m long and $4$ m wide. What is its area?
cues.working: $A = 5.5 \times 4 = 22$ m². B is the perimeter, and C adds the length and width.

m204-7-2-b.title: Area, Part 2: Area of a Triangle

cues.prompt: A triangular sail has a base of $8$ m and a height of $5$ m. What is its area?
cues.working: $A = 8 \times 5 \div 2 = 40 \div 2 = 20$ m². B forgets to divide by $2$, and C adds the base and height.

m204-7-2-c.title: Area, Part 3: Area of a Parallelogram

cues.prompt: A parallelogram has a base of $7$ m and a height of $4$ m. Its slanted sides are $5$ m long. What is its area?
cues.working: $A = b \times h = 7 \times 4 = 28$ m². B uses the slanted side, C divides by $2$ like a triangle, and D multiplies all three numbers.

m204-7-2-d.title: Area, Part 4: Area of a Circle

cues.prompt: A round rug has a diameter of $4$ m. What is its area, to the nearest tenth?
cues.working: $r = 4 \div 2 = 2$ m. $A = \pi \times 2 \times 2 \approx 12.57$ m². B uses the diameter, and C is the circumference, a length.

m204-7-3.title: Composite Shapes, Part 1: Adding the Parts

cues.prompt: An L-shaped deck splits into a $5$ m by $3$ m rectangle and a $4$ m by $2$ m rectangle. What is its total area?
cues.working: $5 \times 3 = 15$ and $4 \times 2 = 8$, so $15 + 8 = 23$ m². B multiplies the two areas, C adds the four lengths, and D is only one part.

m204-7-3-b.title: Composite Shapes, Part 2: Taking Away and Half Circles

chapters.title: A stage with a rounded front

cues.prompt: A yard is $10$ m by $6$ m. A pond that is $2$ m by $1.5$ m is in the yard. What area of grass is left?
cues.working: Yard: $10 \times 6 = 60$ m². Pond: $2 \times 1.5 = 3$ m². Grass: $60 - 3 = 57$ m². B adds the pond, C forgets it, and D is the pond.

m204-7-3-c.title: Composite Shapes, Part 3: How Much Material to Buy

cues.prompt: A lawn is $5$ m by $5$ m. One roll of sod covers $0.8$ m². How many rolls are needed?
cues.working: Area: $5 \times 5 = 25$ m². $25 \div 0.8 = 31.25$, so round up to $32$ rolls. B rounds down, C multiplies, and D cannot be bought.

m204-7-3-d.title: Composite Shapes, Part 4: Waste and GST

chapters.title: Add the waste to the area

cues.prompt: A floor is $20$ m². Add $10\%$ for waste. Each box covers $2.5$ m² and costs \$30.00. GST is $5\%$. What is the total cost?
cues.working: $20 \times 1.1 = 22$ m². $22 \div 2.5 = 8.8$, so $9$ boxes. $9 \times 30 = 270.00$. GST: $13.50$. Total: $283.50$. B forgets GST, C forgets the waste, and D is the GST only.

m204-8-1.title: Scale Drawings, Part 1: What a Scale Means

chapters.title: The size of a living room

cues.prompt: On a floor plan, $1$ cm represents $2$ m. A bedroom is $2.5$ cm long on the plan. How long is the real bedroom?
cues.working: $2.5 \times 2 = 5$ m. B divides, and C adds.

m204-8-1-b.title: Scale Drawings, Part 2: Measuring a Plan

chapters.title: A wall on a garage plan

cues.prompt: A line on a plan starts at the $2$ cm mark and ends at the $8.5$ cm mark. On the plan, $1$ cm represents $3$ m. How long is the real wall?
cues.working: Plan length: $8.5 - 2 = 6.5$ cm. Real: $6.5 \times 3 = 19.5$ m. B uses only the end mark, C is the plan length, and D adds the marks.

cues.prompt: A deck plan uses a scale of $1 : 40$. The deck is $9$ cm long on the plan. How long is the real deck, in metres?
cues.working: $9 \times 40 = 360$ cm, and $360 \div 100 = 3.6$ m. B forgets to change centimetres to metres, and C divides.

m204-8-1-d.title: Scale Drawings, Part 4: Finding the Scale and the Area

cues.prompt: A model boat is $30$ cm long. The real boat is $9$ m long. What is the scale?
cues.working: $9$ m $= 900$ cm. $900 \div 30 = 30$, so the scale is $1 : 30$. B divides $9$ by $30$, mixing metres and centimetres, and D multiplies.

cues.prompt: A map has a scale of $1 : 500\,000$. Two lakes are $4$ cm apart on the map. How far apart are they?
cues.working: $1$ cm represents $500\,000 \div 100\,000 = 5$ km. $4 \times 5 = 20$ km. B forgets to change centimetres to kilometres, and C is the distance for $1$ cm.

m204-8-2-b.title: Maps, Part 2: Routes with Several Legs

cues.prompt: A route has three legs: $2.4$ cm, $1.8$ cm and $3.3$ cm on the map. On the map, $1$ cm represents $4$ km. How long is the route?
cues.working: Map total: $2.4 + 1.8 + 3.3 = 7.5$ cm. Real: $7.5 \times 4 = 30$ km. B leaves out the middle leg, and C is the map length.

cues.prompt: On a grid map, a place is in column D and row $3$. How is its square named?
cues.working: Letter first, then number: D3. B writes the number first, and C and D are one square off.

cues.prompt: On a grid map, the Library is in B5 and the Gas station is in E1. Which direction is the Gas station from the Library?
cues.working: Start at the Library (B5). E is to the right (east) and row 1 is down (south): southeast. B is the way back.

m204-8-3.title: Travel Time, Part 1: Speed and Distance

cues.prompt: A bus travels for $4$ hours at an average speed of $75$ km/h. How far does it go?
cues.working: $\text{distance} = 75 \times 4 = 300$ km. B adds, C divides, and D subtracts.

m204-8-3-b.title: Travel Time, Part 2: Finding the Time or the Speed

cues.prompt: A truck drives $360$ km at an average speed of $90$ km/h. How long does the trip take?
cues.working: $\text{time} = 360 \div 90 = 4$ h. Check: $90 \times 4 = 360$. B divides the wrong way, and C multiplies.

m204-8-3-c.title: Travel Time, Part 3: Hours and Minutes

cues.prompt: A driver goes $150$ km at an average speed of $60$ km/h. How long does the trip take, in hours and minutes?
cues.working: $150 \div 60 = 2.5$ h. $0.5 \times 60 = 30$ min, so $2$ h $30$ min. B reads $0.5$ as $50$ minutes, and C as $5$ minutes.

m204-8-3-d.title: Travel Time, Part 4: Planning a Trip

cues.prompt: Omar leaves at 9:15 a.m., drives $240$ km at $80$ km/h, and stops for $20$ minutes for fuel. When does Omar arrive?
cues.working: Driving: $240 \div 80 = 3$ h. 9:15 a.m. $+ 3$ h $=$ 12:15 p.m., then $+ 20$ min $=$ 12:35 p.m. B forgets the stop.

cues.prompt: On a line graph, the grid lines go up by $20$. A point is halfway between the $60$ line and the $80$ line. What value does it show?
cues.working: Halfway between $60$ and $80$ is $(60 + 80) \div 2 = 70$. D reads the line below.

m204-9-1-b.title: Data Displays, Part 2: Circle Graphs and Percents

cues.prompt: Jordan takes home \$2,400 a month. Transport is $15\%$ and Phone is $5\%$. How much more goes to Transport than to Phone?
cues.working: $15\% - 5\% = 10\%$, and $0.10 \times 2400 = 240$. B is the Transport amount, C is the Phone amount, and D is the percent, not dollars.

m204-9-1-c.title: Data Displays, Part 3: Finding a Percent

cues.prompt: A store had $60$ customers in an hour. $45$ paid by card. What percent paid by card?
cues.working: $45 \div 60 = 0.75$, and $0.75 \times 100 = 75\%$. B divides the wrong way, and D is the percent who did not pay by card.

m204-9-1-d.title: Data Displays, Part 4: Making a Circle Graph

cues.prompt: In a survey of $60$ people, $15$ chose hockey. What angle should the hockey slice have?
cues.working: $\tfrac{15}{60} \times 360 = 90^\circ$. B is the percent, $25\%$, and C is the count.

m204-9-2.title: Analyzing Data, Part 1: Comparing Two Data Sets

cues.prompt: Set A is $10, 12, 14$. Set B is $2, 12, 22$. Both have a mean of $12$. What is the range of set B?
cues.working: Range of B: $22 - 2 = 20$. B is the range of set A, and C is the mean. Set B is much more spread out.

m204-9-2-b.title: Analyzing Data, Part 2: Outliers and the Best Measure

cues.prompt: Five workers earn \$15, \$16, \$17, \$18 and \$64 an hour. Which measure best describes a typical wage?
cues.working: \$64 is an outlier, so use the median: \$17. The mean, $130 \div 5 = 26$, is higher than four of the five wages.

cues.prompt: A graph’s axis starts at $50$. The bars show $52$ and $60$, so the second bar looks $5$ times as tall. By about what percent did the value really grow?
cues.working: Increase: $60 - 52 = 8$. Percent: $8 \div 52 \times 100 \approx 15\%$. B and D believe the bars, and C forgets to divide by $52$.

cues.prompt: A town wants to know if people want a new swimming pool. Which survey is **biased**?
choices: asking only people at the old pool
asking every 10th name on the voters’ list
asking people at many different places in town
cues.working: People at the pool already swim, so they are likely to want a new one. The other surveys reach a fair mix of the town.

cues.prompt: A regular die is rolled once. What is the theoretical probability of rolling a number greater than $4$?
cues.working: Favourable: $5$ and $6$, so $2$. Total: $6$. $P = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}$. C counts the numbers $4$ or less, and D counts only one number.

cues.prompt: Use the coffee shop data: $84$ of $200$ customers ordered a medium. What is the experimental probability of a medium?
cues.working: $\dfrac{84}{200} = 0.42 = 42\%$. B forgets to divide by $200$, C assumes the four sizes are equally likely, and D is the percent who did not order a medium.

cues.prompt: The coffee shop’s records show $P(\text{small}) = 23\%$. About how many of $300$ customers will order a small?
cues.working: $0.23 \times 300 = 69$. B is the percent, C multiplies by $10$, and D assumes the four sizes are equally likely.

m204-9-3-d.title: Probability, Part 4: Comparing Predictions with Results

cues.prompt: In Kai’s $120$ rolls, a $5$ came up $17$ times. The prediction was $20$. How does the real result compare?
cues.working: $20 - 17 = 3$, so $3$ fewer than predicted. That is normal for $120$ rolls.

m301-1-1.title: Horizontal and Vertical Translations, Part 1: Sliding a Graph

cues.prompt: The graph of $y = x^2$ is translated 4 units right and 1 unit down. Which is the equation of the image?
cues.working: Right 4: $h = 4$, so replace $x$ with $x - 4$. Down 1: $k = -1$, so subtract 1.

m301-1-1-b.title: Horizontal and Vertical Translations, Part 2: Image Points and Equations

cues.prompt: The point $(-2, 6)$ is on the graph of $y = f(x)$. What is the corresponding point on the graph of $y = f(x + 4) - 1$?

m301-1-1-c.title: Horizontal and Vertical Translations, Part 3: Domain, Range and Graphs

chapters.title: Reading h and k from graphs

cues.prompt: $y = f(x)$ has domain $\{x \mid 0 \le x \le 6,\ x \in \mathbb{R}\}$ and range $\{y \mid 1 \le y \le 3,\ y \in \mathbb{R}\}$. What is the range of $y = f(x - 2) + 5$?
cues.working: $k = 5$, so the range moves up 5: $1 + 5 = 6$ and $3 + 5 = 8$. The horizontal shift, $h = 2$, changes only the domain.

m301-1-2.title: Reflections and Stretches, Part 1: Reflections in the Axes

cues.prompt: The point $(3, -7)$ is on the graph of $y = f(x)$. Which point is on the graph of $y = f(-x)$?
cues.working: $y = f(-x)$ is a reflection in the $y$-axis: $(x, y) \to (-x, y)$, so $(3, -7) \to (-3, -7)$.

m301-1-2-b.title: Reflections and Stretches, Part 2: Vertical Stretches

cues.prompt: The point $(-1, 5)$ is on the graph of $y = f(x)$. Which point is on the graph of $y = -4f(x)$?
cues.working: $(x, y) \to (x, -4y)$: $-4(5) = -20$, and $x$ does not change.

m301-1-2-c.title: Reflections and Stretches, Part 3: Horizontal Stretches

cues.prompt: The point $(8, 3)$ is on the graph of $y = f(x)$. Which point is on the graph of $y = f(4x)$?
cues.working: $(x, y) \to \left(\frac{x}{4},\ y\right)$: $\frac{8}{4} = 2$, and $y$ does not change.

m301-1-2-d.title: Reflections and Stretches, Part 4: Invariant Points

cues.prompt: Let $f(x) = x^2 + 2x - 8 = (x + 4)(x - 2)$. Which points are invariant for $y = -3f(x)$?
cues.working: $y = -3f(x)$ is a vertical stretch and a reflection in the $x$-axis, so the points with $y = 0$ stay put: the $x$-intercepts $(-4, 0)$ and $(2, 0)$.

m301-1-3.title: Combining Transformations, Part 1: The General Form

cues.prompt: The point $(4, 3)$ is on the graph of $y = f(x)$. What is the corresponding point on the graph of $y = 2f(4(x + 1)) - 5$?

m301-1-3-b.title: Combining Transformations, Part 2: Describing and Factoring

cues.prompt: What is the horizontal translation in $y = f(3x + 12)$?
The graph of $y = x^2$ is stretched vertically by a factor of $2$, reflected in the $x$-axis, and translated 1 unit left and 3 units up. Which is its equation?
cues.working: $a = -2$ (a stretch by $2$ and a reflection in the $x$-axis), $h = -1$ and $k = 3$.

m301-1-4.title: Inverse of a Relation, Part 1: Interchanging x and y

cues.prompt: A function $f$ has domain $\{x \mid x \ge 2\}$ and range $\{y \mid y \le 5\}$. What is the domain of $f^{-1}$?
cues.working: The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$: all values at most $5$.

m301-1-4-b.title: Inverse of a Relation, Part 2: Finding an Inverse Algebraically

cues.prompt: Find the inverse of $f(x) = 5x + 2$.
cues.working: Interchange: $x = 5y + 2$. Then $5y = x - 2$, so $y = \dfrac{x - 2}{5}$.

m301-1-4-c.title: Inverse of a Relation, Part 3: The Horizontal Line Test

cues.prompt: Let $f(x) = (x + 1)^2 - 4$ with $x \le -1$. Which is $f^{-1}(x)$?
cues.working: Interchange: $(y + 1)^2 = x + 4$, so $y = -1 \pm \sqrt{x + 4}$. The left half ($x \le -1$) means the inverse needs $y \le -1$: the negative root.

m301-2-1.title: Radical Functions and Transformations, Part 1: The Square Root Function

cues.prompt: Which point is **not** on the graph of $y = \sqrt{x}$?
cues.working: $\sqrt{4}$ is the principal square root, $2$, never $-2$: the range is $y \ge 0$. The others work: $\sqrt{16} = 4$, $\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$ and $\sqrt{0} = 0$.

m301-2-1-b.title: Radical Functions and Transformations, Part 2: Mapping the Key Points

cues.prompt: The point $(4, 2)$ is on $y = \sqrt{x}$. Where is its image on the graph of $y = 3\sqrt{x + 1} - 2$?

m301-2-1-c.title: Radical Functions and Transformations, Part 3: Domain and Range

cues.prompt: State the domain and range of $y = 2\sqrt{8 - 2x} - 1$.
cues.working: $8 - 2x = -2(x - 4)$, so the endpoint is $(4, -1)$. $b = -2 < 0$: domain $\{x \mid x \le 4,\ x \in \mathbb{R}\}$. $a = 2 > 0$: range $\{y \mid y \ge -1,\ y \in \mathbb{R}\}$.

m301-2-1-d.title: Radical Functions and Transformations, Part 4: Equations from Graphs

cues.prompt: The graph of a radical function has its endpoint at $(1, -2)$, opens to the right, and passes through $(5, 4)$. Which is its equation?

m301-2-2.title: Square Root of a Function, Part 1: Invariant Points

cues.prompt: Let $f(x) = x + 3$. What are the invariant points of the graph of $y = \sqrt{f(x)}$?
cues.working: $f(x) = 0$ when $x = -3$, and $f(x) = 1$ when $x = -2$. At those $x$-values, $\sqrt{f(x)} = f(x)$.

m301-2-2-b.title: Square Root of a Function, Part 2: Domain, Range and Quadratics

cues.prompt: What is the domain of $y = \sqrt{x^2 - 9}$?
cues.working: $x^2 - 9 = (x + 3)(x - 3)$ has zeros $-3$ and $3$, and the parabola opens up, so $x^2 - 9 \ge 0$ outside the zeros: $x \le -3$ or $x \ge 3$.

m301-2-2-c.title: Square Root of a Function, Part 3: Arches and Quick Sketches

cues.prompt: What is the range of $y = \sqrt{16 - x^2}$?
cues.working: The maximum of $16 - x^2$ is $16$, at $x = 0$, so the maximum of $\sqrt{16 - x^2}$ is $\sqrt{16} = 4$. The smallest value is $0$, at $x = \pm 4$.

m301-2-3.title: Solving Radical Equations Graphically, Part 1: Two Graphical Methods

cues.prompt: To solve $\sqrt{x + 6} = 3$ with the related function, which function do you graph, and what is the solution?
cues.working: Subtract $3$: $\sqrt{x + 6} - 3 = 0$. The graph of $y = \sqrt{x + 6} - 3$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x = 3$. Check: $\sqrt{3 + 6} = \sqrt{9} = 3$.

m301-2-3-b.title: Solving Radical Equations Graphically, Part 2: Extraneous Roots

cues.prompt: Solve $\sqrt{x + 5} = x - 1$.

m301-2-3-c.title: Solving Radical Equations Graphically, Part 3: Approximate Solutions and Applications

cues.prompt: The time $t$, in seconds, for a stone to fall $d$ metres is modelled by $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{d}{4.9}}$. A stone falls for $2$ s. How far does it fall?
cues.working: Square both sides of $\sqrt{\dfrac{d}{4.9}} = 2$: $\dfrac{d}{4.9} = 4$, so $d = 4 \times 4.9 = 19.6$ m. Check: $\sqrt{\dfrac{19.6}{4.9}} = \sqrt{4} = 2$.

m301-3-1.title: Characteristics of Polynomial Functions, Part 1: Degree and Leading Coefficient

cues.prompt: State the degree and the leading coefficient of $g(x) = 5x + 2x^3 - 4x^4 + 9$.
cues.working: In descending order, $g(x) = -4x^4 + 2x^3 + 5x + 9$: the degree is $4$ and the leading coefficient is $-4$.

m301-3-1-b.title: Characteristics of Polynomial Functions, Part 2: End Behaviour

cues.prompt: Describe the end behaviour of $y = -2x^3 + x^2 + 5$.
cues.working: The leading term is $-2x^3$. The degree is odd, so the ends go opposite ways; the leading coefficient is negative, so the right end falls. It rises to the left and falls to the right.

m301-3-1-c.title: Characteristics of Polynomial Functions, Part 3: Intercepts and Turning Points

cues.prompt: A polynomial function has degree $4$. Which statement must be true?
cues.working: Degree $4$ allows at most $4 - 1 = 3$ turning points and at most $4$ $x$-intercepts. The degree is even, so it may have no $x$-intercepts at all.

m301-3-2.title: The Remainder Theorem, Part 1: Polynomial Long Division

cues.prompt: Divide $x^3 + 3x^2 - x + 4$ by $x + 2$. Find the quotient and the remainder.
