cues.working: $x^3 \div x = x^2$; subtract $x^3 + 2x^2$ to get $x^2 - x$. $x^2 \div x = x$; subtract $x^2 + 2x$ to get $-3x + 4$. $-3x \div x = -3$; subtract $-3x - 6$ to get $10$.

m301-3-2-b.title: The Remainder Theorem, Part 2: Synthetic Division

cues.prompt: Use synthetic division to divide $x^3 - 4x + 5$ by $x - 3$.
cues.working: Coefficients $1, 0, -4, 5$ and $a = 3$: bring down $1$; $0 + 3 = 3$; $-4 + 9 = 5$; $5 + 15 = 20$. The quotient starts at $x^2$.

m301-3-2-c.title: The Remainder Theorem, Part 3: Remainders Without Dividing

cues.prompt: Find the remainder when $P(x) = 2x^3 - x^2 + 3x - 4$ is divided by $x + 2$.

m301-3-2-d.title: The Remainder Theorem, Part 4: Unknown Coefficients

cues.prompt: When $P(x) = 2x^3 + kx^2 - x + 5$ is divided by $x + 1$, the remainder is $8$. Find $k$.

m301-3-3.title: The Factor Theorem, Part 1: A Remainder of Zero

cues.prompt: Which binomial is a factor of $P(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 - x - 2$?

m301-3-3-b.title: The Factor Theorem, Part 2: The Integral Zero Theorem

cues.prompt: Which of these is **not** a possible integral zero of $P(x) = x^3 + 4x^2 - 3x - 10$?
cues.working: The constant term is $-10$, so the possible integral zeros are $\pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 5, \pm 10$. $4$ does not divide $-10$.

m301-3-3-c.title: The Factor Theorem, Part 3: Factoring Higher Degrees

cues.prompt: Factor $P(x) = x^3 - 7x - 6$ completely.

m301-3-3-d.title: The Factor Theorem, Part 4: Grouping and Unknown Coefficients

cues.prompt: Find $k$ so that $x - 3$ is a factor of $P(x) = x^3 - 2x^2 + kx + 6$.

m301-3-4.title: Equations and Graphs of Polynomial Functions, Part 1: Solving by Factoring

m301-3-4-b.title: Equations and Graphs of Polynomial Functions, Part 2: Multiplicity

cues.prompt: At which zero does $y = (x - 4)^2(x + 1)$ touch the $x$-axis?
cues.working: $(x - 4)^2$ gives the zero $4$ with multiplicity $2$, so the graph touches there. At $-1$ the multiplicity is $1$, so it crosses.

m301-3-4-c.title: Equations and Graphs of Polynomial Functions, Part 3: Sketching from Factored Form

cues.prompt: Find the $y$-intercept and the end behaviour of $y = (x - 2)^2(x + 3)$.
cues.working: $y$-intercept: $(0 - 2)^2(0 + 3) = 4 \times 3 = 12$. Degree $2 + 1 = 3$, odd, and leading coefficient $1$: from quadrant III to quadrant I.

m301-3-4-d.title: Equations and Graphs of Polynomial Functions, Part 4: Equations from Graphs

cues.prompt: A cubic function has a zero of multiplicity $2$ at $x = 3$, a zero of multiplicity $1$ at $x = -1$, and a $y$-intercept of $18$. Which is its equation?

m301-3-4-e.title: Equations and Graphs of Polynomial Functions, Part 5: Inequalities and Applications

chapters.title: A box with a given volume

cues.working: The zeros $-1$, $2$ and $4$ split the line. $P(-2) = -24$, $P(0) = 8$, $P(3) = -4$ and $P(5) = 18$, so $P(x) < 0$ on $(-\infty, -1)$ and $(2, 4)$. The zeros are not included.

m301-4-1.title: Angles and Angle Measure, Part 1: Radian Measure

cues.prompt: Convert $150^\circ$ to radians. Give an exact answer.
cues.working: $150^\circ \times \dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ} = \dfrac{150\pi}{180} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, dividing the numerator and denominator by $30$.

m301-4-1-b.title: Angles and Angle Measure, Part 2: Coterminal Angles

cues.prompt: Which angle is coterminal with $\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$?
cues.working: Subtract a full turn, $2\pi = \dfrac{6\pi}{3}$: $\dfrac{5\pi}{3} - \dfrac{6\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

m301-4-1-c.title: Angles and Angle Measure, Part 3: Arc Length

cues.prompt: A circle has a radius of $10$ cm. How long is the arc subtended by a central angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$, to the nearest tenth of a centimetre?
cues.working: $a = r\theta = 10 \times \dfrac{\pi}{5} = 2\pi \approx 6.28$, so about $6.3$ cm.

m301-4-2.title: The Unit Circle, Part 1: The Equation of the Unit Circle

chapters.title: Is the point on the circle?

cues.prompt: The point $\left(\dfrac{3}{5}, y\right)$ is on the unit circle in quadrant IV. Determine $y$.
cues.working: $y^2 = 1 - \dfrac{9}{25} = \dfrac{16}{25}$, so $y = \pm\dfrac{4}{5}$. In quadrant IV, $y < 0$: $y = -\dfrac{4}{5}$.

m301-4-2-b.title: The Unit Circle, Part 2: Points for Special Angles

cues.prompt: What is the exact value of $\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}$?
cues.working: $P\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$, and $\cos\theta$ is the $x$-coordinate: $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

m301-4-2-c.title: The Unit Circle, Part 3: Points in Every Quadrant

chapters.title: From a point to the angle

cues.prompt: Determine the exact coordinates of $P\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)$.
cues.working: $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ is in quadrant II with reference angle $\pi - \dfrac{5\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$. $P\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$; in quadrant II, $x < 0$ and $y > 0$.

m301-4-2-d.title: The Unit Circle, Part 4: Symmetry and Larger Circles

cues.prompt: $P(\theta) = \left(-\dfrac{8}{17}, \dfrac{15}{17}\right)$. Determine $P(-\theta)$.
cues.working: $-\theta$ reflects $P(\theta)$ in the $x$-axis: $x$ stays the same and $y$ changes sign.

m301-4-3.title: Trigonometric Ratios, Part 1: The Six Ratios

cues.prompt: $P(\theta) = \left(\dfrac{5}{13}, -\dfrac{12}{13}\right)$. What is $\csc\theta$?
cues.working: $\sin\theta = y = -\dfrac{12}{13}$, so $\csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{y} = -\dfrac{13}{12}$.

m301-4-3-b.title: Trigonometric Ratios, Part 2: Exact Values for Special Angles

cues.prompt: Determine the exact value of $\csc\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.
cues.working: $P\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$, so $\csc\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{y} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$.

m301-4-3-c.title: Trigonometric Ratios, Part 3: From One Ratio to the Others

cues.prompt: $\cot\theta = \dfrac{3}{4}$ and $\theta$ terminates in quadrant III. Determine $\sin\theta$.
cues.working: In quadrant III, $x < 0$ and $y < 0$: $\cot\theta = \dfrac{x}{y} = \dfrac{-3}{-4}$. Then $r = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$, so $\sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{r} = -\dfrac{4}{5}$.

m301-4-3-d.title: Trigonometric Ratios, Part 4: Calculator Values and Angles

cues.prompt: Determine $\cot 5$ to the nearest thousandth.
cues.working: Radian mode: $\tan 5 \approx -3.38052$, so $\cot 5 = \dfrac{1}{\tan 5} \approx -0.296$.

m301-4-4.title: Introduction to Trigonometric Equations, Part 1: Solving Over One Rotation

cues.prompt: Solve $2\sin\theta - \sqrt{3} = 0$ for $0 \le \theta < 2\pi$.
cues.working: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so $\theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$. Sine is positive in quadrants I and II: $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ or $\theta = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

m301-4-4-b.title: Introduction to Trigonometric Equations, Part 2: When the Value Is Not Special

cues.prompt: Solve $4\cos\theta - 1 = 0$ for $0 \le \theta < 2\pi$, to the nearest hundredth.
cues.working: $\cos\theta = 0.25$, so $\theta_R = \cos^{-1}(0.25) \approx 1.3181$. Cosine is positive in quadrants I and IV: $\theta \approx 1.32$ or $\theta = 2\pi - 1.3181 \approx 4.97$.

m301-4-4-c.title: Introduction to Trigonometric Equations, Part 3: Larger Domains and the General Solution

cues.prompt: Write the general solution of $\sqrt{3}\tan\theta - 1 = 0$, where $n \in \mathbb{I}$.
cues.working: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, so $\theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$. Tangent is positive in quadrants I and III: $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$, which are $\pi$ apart.

m301-5-1.title: Graphing Sine and Cosine Functions, Part 1: From the Unit Circle to the Graphs

cues.prompt: For $0 \le x \le 2\pi$, at which value of $x$ does $y = \sin x$ reach its minimum?
cues.working: $\sin x$ is the height of $P(x)$ on the unit circle. $P$ is lowest, at $(0, -1)$, when $x = \frac{3\pi}{2}$, so the minimum value $-1$ is at $x = \frac{3\pi}{2}$.

m301-5-1-b.title: Graphing Sine and Cosine Functions, Part 2: Domain, Range, Zeros and Maximums

cues.prompt: Determine the $x$-values of the maximums of $y = \cos x$ for $0 \le x \le 4\pi$.
cues.working: The maximums of $y = \cos x$ are at $x = 2\pi n$, where $P(x)$ is at $(1, 0)$. From $0$ to $4\pi$ that gives $x = 0$, $2\pi$ and $4\pi$.

m301-5-1-c.title: Graphing Sine and Cosine Functions, Part 3: Amplitude, the Effect of a

cues.prompt: State the amplitude and range of $y = -4\sin x$.
cues.working: $a = -4$, so the amplitude is $\lvert -4 \rvert = 4$, and the graph is reflected in the $x$-axis. It goes from $-4$ to $4$: the range is $\{y \mid -4 \le y \le 4,\ y \in \mathbb{R}\}$.

m301-5-1-d.title: Graphing Sine and Cosine Functions, Part 4: Period, the Effect of b

cues.prompt: Determine the period of $y = 5\sin 4x$.
cues.working: $b = 4$, so the period is $\frac{2\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2}$. The $5$ is the amplitude; it does not change the period.

m301-5-2.title: Transformations of Sinusoidal Functions, Part 1: The Four Parameters

cues.prompt: State the phase shift and range of $y = 5\cos\left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) - 2$.
cues.working: $x + \frac{\pi}{4} = x - \left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$, so the graph moves $\frac{\pi}{4}$ left. The midline is $y = -2$ and the amplitude is $5$: from $-2 - 5 = -7$ to $-2 + 5 = 3$.

m301-5-2-b.title: Transformations of Sinusoidal Functions, Part 2: Factor b First

cues.prompt: What is the phase shift of $y = \sin\left(2x - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$?
cues.working: Factor out $2$: $2x - \frac{\pi}{2} = 2\left(x - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)$, so $c = \frac{\pi}{4}$: a shift of $\frac{\pi}{4}$ to the right.

m301-5-2-c.title: Transformations of Sinusoidal Functions, Part 3: Writing an Equation from a Graph

cues.prompt: A sinusoidal graph has a maximum of $5$ at $x = \frac{\pi}{2}$, and its next minimum, $-1$, at $x = \frac{3\pi}{2}$. Which equation fits the graph?
cues.working: $a = \frac{5 - (-1)}{2} = 3$ and $d = \frac{5 + (-1)}{2} = 2$. From a maximum to the next minimum is half a period, so the period is $2\pi$ and $b = 1$. A maximum at $x = \frac{\pi}{2}$ gives $c = \frac{\pi}{2}$.

m301-5-2-d.title: Transformations of Sinusoidal Functions, Part 4: Writing an Equation from a Description

cues.prompt: A cosine function has an amplitude of $2$, a period of $\pi$, a phase shift of $\frac{\pi}{3}$ to the left and a vertical displacement of $1$ down. Which is its equation?
cues.working: $a = 2$ and $d = -1$. $b = \frac{2\pi}{\pi} = 2$. A shift of $\frac{\pi}{3}$ to the left means $c = -\frac{\pi}{3}$, so the bracket is $\left(x + \frac{\pi}{3}\right)$.

m301-5-3.title: The Tangent Function, Part 1: Tangent on the Unit Circle

cues.prompt: The terminal arm of $\theta$ meets the unit circle at $P\left(\frac{3}{5}, -\frac{4}{5}\right)$. Determine $\tan\theta$.
cues.working: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{-4/5}{3/5} = -\dfrac{4}{3}$, the slope of the terminal arm.

m301-5-3-b.title: The Tangent Function, Part 2: The Graph of y = tan x

chapters.title: Asymptotes and zeros in an interval

cues.prompt: State the period and range of $y = \tan x$.
cues.working: The arms at $\theta$ and $\theta + \pi$ lie on the same line, so they have the same slope: the period is $\pi$. A slope can be any real number, so the range is all real numbers.

m301-5-3-c.title: The Tangent Function, Part 3: Solving tan x = k

chapters.title: The period of y = tan bx

cues.prompt: Solve $\tan x = 3$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$, to the nearest hundredth.
cues.working: $\tan^{-1} 3 \approx 1.2490$, which is in the domain. Adding $\pi$ gives $\approx 4.3906$; adding $2\pi$ gives $\approx 7.5322$, which is past $2\pi$.

m301-5-4.title: Equations and Graphs of Trigonometric Functions, Part 1: Building a Model

cues.prompt: A Ferris wheel has a radius of $15$ m, its centre is $17$ m above the ground, and it makes one rotation every $40$ s. A rider boards at the lowest point at $t = 0$. Which equation models the rider’s height?
cues.working: $|a| = 15$ (the radius) and $d = 17$ (the centre). The rider starts at a minimum, so use $-\cos$: $a = -15$. $b = \frac{2\pi}{40} = \frac{\pi}{20}$.

m301-5-4-b.title: Equations and Graphs of Trigonometric Functions, Part 2: When Does It Reach a Value?

cues.prompt: For $h(t) = -20\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{30}t\right) + 22$, when during the first rotation ($0 \le t \le 60$) is the rider $12$ m above the ground?
cues.working: $\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{30}t\right) = \frac{12 - 22}{-20} = 0.5$, so $\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$ or $2\pi - \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{5\pi}{3}$. Then $t = \frac{30\theta}{\pi}$ gives $t = 10$ or $t = 50$.

m301-5-4-c.title: Equations and Graphs of Trigonometric Functions, Part 3: Daylight in Edmonton

cues.prompt: Use $L(t) = 4.9\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{365}(t - 80)\right) + 12.2$ to estimate the hours of daylight on day $200$.
cues.working: $\frac{2\pi}{365}(200 - 80) \approx 2.0657$, and $\sin 2.0657 \approx 0.8803$ in radian mode, so $L(200) \approx 4.9(0.8803) + 12.2 \approx 16.5$.

m301-6-1.title: Reciprocal, Quotient and Pythagorean Identities, Part 1: Identities and Non-Permissible Values

cues.prompt: Which gives **all** the non-permissible values of $\dfrac{\tan x}{1 + \sin x}$ for $0 \le x < 2\pi$?
cues.working: $1 + \sin x = 0$ when $\sin x = -1$: $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$. And $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ is undefined when $\cos x = 0$: $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

m301-6-1-b.title: Reciprocal, Quotient and Pythagorean Identities, Part 2: Reciprocal and Quotient Identities

chapters.title: Why sin x over tan x is cos x

cues.prompt: Simplify $\sec x\cot x$.
cues.working: $\sec x\cot x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}\cdot\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x} = \dfrac{1}{\sin x} = \csc x$

m301-6-1-c.title: Reciprocal, Quotient and Pythagorean Identities, Part 3: The Pythagorean Identities

cues.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{1 - \cos^2 x}{\sin x\cos x}$.
cues.working: $1 - \cos^2 x = \sin^2 x$, so $\dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\sin x\cos x} = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \tan x$.

m301-6-1-d.title: Reciprocal, Quotient and Pythagorean Identities, Part 4: Simplifying Harder Expressions

cues.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{1}{\cos x} - \sin x\tan x$.
cues.working: $\dfrac{1}{\cos x} - \dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\cos x} = \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 x}{\cos x} = \dfrac{\cos^2 x}{\cos x} = \cos x$

m301-6-2.title: Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Identities, Part 1: The Sum and Difference Identities

chapters.title: Writing an expansion as one function

cues.prompt: Determine the exact value of $\sin 80^\circ\cos 20^\circ - \cos 80^\circ\sin 20^\circ$.
cues.working: This is $\sin A\cos B - \cos A\sin B = \sin(A - B)$ with $A = 80^\circ$ and $B = 20^\circ$: $\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

m301-6-2-b.title: Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Identities, Part 2: Exact Values

cues.prompt: Determine the exact value of $\cos 15^\circ$.
cues.working: $\cos(45^\circ - 30^\circ) = \cos 45^\circ\cos 30^\circ + \sin 45^\circ\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{4} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4} = \dfrac{\sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2}}{4}$

m301-6-2-c.title: Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Identities, Part 3: Double-Angle Identities

chapters.title: From one ratio and a quadrant

cues.prompt: Given $\cos\theta = \dfrac{5}{13}$ with $\dfrac{3\pi}{2} < \theta < 2\pi$, determine $\sin 2\theta$.
cues.working: In quadrant IV, $y = -\sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = -12$, so $\sin\theta = -\dfrac{12}{13}$. Then $\sin 2\theta = 2\left(-\dfrac{12}{13}\right)\left(\dfrac{5}{13}\right) = -\dfrac{120}{169}$.

m301-6-2-d.title: Sum, Difference and Double-Angle Identities, Part 4: Two Angles from Given Ratios

chapters.title: The cosine of A minus B

cues.prompt: With $\sin A = \dfrac{4}{5}$, $A$ in quadrant II, and $\cos B = \dfrac{5}{13}$, $B$ in quadrant IV, as before, determine $\sin(A - B)$.
cues.working: Use $\sin(A - B) = \sin A\cos B - \cos A\sin B$: $\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)\left(\dfrac{5}{13}\right) - \left(-\dfrac{3}{5}\right)\left(-\dfrac{12}{13}\right)$, which is $\dfrac{20}{65} - \dfrac{36}{65} = -\dfrac{16}{65}$.

m301-6-3.title: Proving Identities, Part 1: Checking with Numbers and Graphs

cues.prompt: Which value of $x$ is a counterexample that shows $\cos 2x = 2\cos x - 1$ is **not** an identity?
cues.working: At $x = 60^\circ$: $\cos 120^\circ = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, but $2\cos 60^\circ - 1 = 0$. At $0^\circ$, $90^\circ$ and $360^\circ$ the two sides are equal, so they cannot show it.

m301-6-3-b.title: Proving Identities, Part 2: Proving an Identity with Algebra

cues.prompt: To prove $\dfrac{\cos x}{1 + \sin x} = \dfrac{1 - \sin x}{\cos x}$, which first step is valid?
choices: Multiply the left side by $\dfrac{1 - \sin x}{1 - \sin x}$
Cancel the $1$s on the left: $\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$
cues.working: Left side $= \dfrac{\cos x(1 - \sin x)}{1 - \sin^2 x} = \dfrac{\cos x(1 - \sin x)}{\cos^2 x} = \dfrac{1 - \sin x}{\cos x}$, the right side.

m301-6-3-c.title: Proving Identities, Part 3: Double Angles and Non-Permissible Values

chapters.title: A proof with a double angle

cues.prompt: What are the non-permissible values of the identity $\dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x} = \csc x - \cot x$?

m301-6-3-d.title: Proving Identities, Part 4: Finding the Error in a Proof

cues.prompt: A student works on the left side of $\sec^2 x - \tan^2 x + \cot^2 x = \csc^2 x$, gets $\sec^2 x$, and decides it is not an identity. Which step has the first error?
choices: No error: it is not an identity.
cues.working: $1 + \cot^2 x = \csc^2 x$, not $\sec^2 x$: Step 3 uses the wrong Pythagorean identity. The left side does equal $\csc^2 x$, so it is an identity.

m301-6-4.title: Solving Trigonometric Equations Using Identities, Part 1: Quadratic Equations in One Function

cues.prompt: Solve $2\cos^2 x + \cos x - 1 = 0$ for $0 \le x < 2\pi$.

m301-6-4-b.title: Solving Trigonometric Equations Using Identities, Part 2: Square Roots, Impossible Values and Calculator Values

cues.prompt: Solve $2\sin^2 x - 1 = 0$ for $0^\circ \le x < 360^\circ$.
cues.working: $\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\sin x = \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$. Positive: $45^\circ,\ 135^\circ$. Negative: $225^\circ,\ 315^\circ$.

m301-6-4-c.title: Solving Trigonometric Equations Using Identities, Part 3: Using an Identity First

cues.prompt: Solve $\sin 2x = \cos x$ for $0^\circ \le x < 360^\circ$.
cues.working: $2\sin x\cos x - \cos x = 0$, so $\cos x(2\sin x - 1) = 0$. $\cos x = 0$: $90^\circ,\ 270^\circ$. $\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2}$: $30^\circ,\ 150^\circ$.

m301-6-4-d.title: Solving Trigonometric Equations Using Identities, Part 4: General Solutions

cues.prompt: Which is the general solution of $\sin^2 x = \sin x$, with $n \in \mathrm{I}$?
cues.working: In one revolution: $x = 0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \pi$. $0$ and $\pi$ are a half-turn apart: $\pi n$. $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ repeats every $2\pi$: $\dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi n$.

m301-7-1.title: Characteristics of Exponential Functions, Part 1: What an Exponential Function Is

cues.prompt: For $f(x) = 9^{x}$, find $f\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)$.
cues.working: $9^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{9^{\frac{1}{2}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$. The negative sign makes a reciprocal; the one half makes a square root.

m301-7-1-b.title: Characteristics of Exponential Functions, Part 2: Growth, Decay and Key Features

cues.prompt: Which function shows exponential **growth**?
cues.working: $\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{-x} = 5^{x}$, and $5 > 1$. The others are decay: $0.9$ and $\frac{2}{3}$ are between $0$ and $1$, and $4^{-x} = \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{x}$.

m301-7-1-c.title: Characteristics of Exponential Functions, Part 3: Finding an Exponential Equation

cues.prompt: An exponential function $y = a(c)^{x}$ passes through $(1, 8)$ and $(3, 32)$. Find its equation.
cues.working: $\dfrac{ac^{3}}{ac} = \dfrac{32}{8}$, so $c^{2} = 4$ and $c = 2$ (the base is positive). Then $8 = 2a$, so $a = 4$.

m301-7-2.title: Transformations of Exponential Functions, Part 1: The Transformation Equation

cues.prompt: State the range of $y = -4(3)^{x - 1} + 2$.
cues.working: $k = 2$, so the asymptote is $y = 2$. Because $a = -4 < 0$, the graph is reflected in the $x$-axis and lies below the asymptote: $y < 2$.

m301-7-2-b.title: Transformations of Exponential Functions, Part 2: Image Points

cues.prompt: The point $(1, 3)$ is on $y = 3^{x}$. Find its image on $y = 2(3)^{\frac{1}{3}(x - 2)} - 1$.

m301-7-2-c.title: Transformations of Exponential Functions, Part 3: Writing the Equation

cues.prompt: The graph of $y = 2^{x}$ is reflected in the $x$-axis, stretched horizontally by a factor of $\frac{1}{3}$ and translated $5$ units right. Write the equation.
cues.working: Reflection in the $x$-axis: $a = -1$. Horizontal stretch by $\frac{1}{3}$: $b = \dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{3}} = 3$. Right $5$: $h = 5$.

m301-7-3-c.title: Solving Exponential Equations, Part 3: Products, Quotients, Radicals and Half-Life

cues.prompt: An isotope has a half-life of $5$ days, so the mass left from a $96\text{ mg}$ sample is $A = 96\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{t}{5}}$. When will $3\text{ mg}$ remain?
cues.working: $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{t}{5}} = \frac{3}{96} = \frac{1}{32} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{5}$, so $\frac{t}{5} = 5$ and $t = 25$ days.

m301-7-4.title: Understanding Logarithms, Part 1: Logarithms Are Exponents

cues.prompt: Write $5^{-2} = \frac{1}{25}$ in logarithmic form.
cues.working: The base $5$ stays the base, and the exponent $-2$ becomes the value of the logarithm: $\log_{5} \frac{1}{25} = -2$.

m301-7-4-b.title: Understanding Logarithms, Part 2: Evaluating and Estimating Logarithms

cues.prompt: Evaluate $\log_{9} 27$.

m301-7-4-c.title: Understanding Logarithms, Part 3: Solving Equations by Converting

cues.prompt: Solve $\log_{x} 16 = -2$.
cues.working: $x^{-2} = 16$, so $x^{2} = \frac{1}{16}$ and $x = \pm\frac{1}{4}$. The base must be positive, so $x = \frac{1}{4}$.

m301-7-5.title: Transformations of Logarithmic Functions, Part 1: The Inverse of an Exponential Function

cues.prompt: Which point is on the graph of $y = \log_{3} x$?
cues.working: $\log_{3} 9 = 2$, because $3^{2} = 9$. The point $(2, 9)$ is on the inverse, $y = 3^{x}$.

m301-7-5-b.title: Transformations of Logarithmic Functions, Part 2: Transforming Logarithmic Graphs

cues.prompt: State the vertical asymptote and the domain of $y = 3\log\left(-(x + 2)\right) - 1$.
cues.working: The argument must be positive: $-(x + 2) > 0$, so $x + 2 < 0$ and $x < -2$. The asymptote is $x = h = -2$.

m301-7-5-c.title: Transformations of Logarithmic Functions, Part 3: Intercepts, Domains and Inverses

cues.prompt: Find the $x$-intercept of $y = 3\log_{2}(x + 1) - 6$.

m301-7-6-b.title: Laws of Logarithms, Part 2: The Power Law and Change of Base

cues.prompt: Evaluate $\log_{2} 20$ to the nearest hundredth.

m301-7-7.title: Logarithmic and Exponential Equations, Part 1: Solving Logarithmic Equations

cues.working: $x(x - 5) = 6^{2} = 36$, so $x^{2} - 5x - 36 = 0$ and $(x - 9)(x + 4) = 0$. $x = -4$ makes $\log_{6} x$ undefined, so it is extraneous.

m301-7-7-b.title: Logarithmic and Exponential Equations, Part 2: Exponential Equations with Logarithms

cues.prompt: Solve $5(2)^{x} = 35$. Round to the nearest hundredth.
cues.working: $2^{x} = 7$, so $x\log 2 = \log 7$ and $x = \dfrac{\log 7}{\log 2} \approx \dfrac{0.8451}{0.3010} \approx 2.81$.

m301-8-1.title: Exploring Rational Functions, Part 1: The Graph of y = a/(x − h) + k

cues.prompt: What are the asymptotes of $y = \dfrac{4}{x + 2} - 1$?
cues.working: $x + 2 = x - (-2)$, so $h = -2$: the vertical asymptote is $x = -2$. $k = -1$, so the horizontal asymptote is $y = -1$.

m301-8-1-b.title: Exploring Rational Functions, Part 2: Vertical Asymptotes and Holes

chapters.title: Not every zero gives an asymptote

cues.prompt: Which describes the graph of $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x^2 + 2x - 3}$?
choices: A hole at $x = -3$ and a vertical asymptote $x = 1$
A hole at $\left(1, \tfrac{1}{2}\right)$ and a vertical asymptote $x = 3$
A hole at $\left(1, \tfrac{1}{2}\right)$ and a vertical asymptote $x = -3$
cues.working: $f(x) = \dfrac{(x - 1)(x + 1)}{(x + 3)(x - 1)} = \dfrac{x + 1}{x + 3}$, $x \ne 1$. The hole is at $x = 1$, $y = \dfrac{1 + 1}{1 + 3} = \dfrac{1}{2}$; $x + 3$ remains, so $x = -3$ is a vertical asymptote.

m301-8-1-c.title: Exploring Rational Functions, Part 3: Horizontal Asymptotes

cues.prompt: What is the horizontal asymptote of $f(x) = \dfrac{6x^2 + 1}{3x^2 - 2x}$?
cues.working: Both have degree $2$, so the asymptote is the ratio of the leading coefficients: $y = \dfrac{6}{3} = 2$.

m301-8-1-d.title: Exploring Rational Functions, Part 4: Intercepts, Domain and Every Feature

chapters.title: A cancelled zero is not an intercept

cues.prompt: What are the intercepts of $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x^2 - 4x + 3}$?
cues.working: $f(x) = \dfrac{(x - 1)(x + 1)}{(x - 1)(x - 3)} = \dfrac{x + 1}{x - 3}$, $x \ne 1$, so the only $x$-intercept is $-1$ (there is a hole at $x = 1$). $f(0) = \dfrac{-1}{3} = -\dfrac{1}{3}$.

m301-8-2.title: Analyzing Rational Functions, Part 1: Sketching with a Hole

cues.prompt: Where is the hole in the graph of $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 + x - 6}$?

m301-8-2-b.title: Analyzing Rational Functions, Part 2: Two Vertical Asymptotes

cues.prompt: For $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 1}{(x - 3)(x + 4)}$, where is the graph above the $x$-axis?

m301-8-2-c.title: Analyzing Rational Functions, Part 3: Writing an Equation from a Graph

cues.prompt: A graph has a vertical asymptote $x = 3$, a horizontal asymptote $y = -1$, an $x$-intercept of $-2$ and no holes. Which equation fits?
cues.working: $x = 3$ gives $(x - 3)$ in the denominator, the intercept $-2$ gives $(x + 2)$ in the numerator, and equal degrees give the horizontal asymptote $y = a$, so $a = -1$.

m301-8-3.title: Connecting Graphs and Rational Equations, Part 1: Solving Algebraically

cues.prompt: Solve $\dfrac{x + 7}{x - 2} = 4$.
cues.working: $x \ne 2$. Multiply by $x - 2$: $x + 7 = 4x - 8$, so $15 = 3x$ and $x = 5$. Check: $\dfrac{12}{3} = 4$.

m301-8-3-b.title: Connecting Graphs and Rational Equations, Part 2: Extraneous Roots

cues.prompt: Solve $\dfrac{x^2}{x + 3} = \dfrac{9}{x + 3}$.
cues.working: $x \ne -3$. Multiply by $x + 3$: $x^2 = 9$, so $x = \pm 3$. $x = -3$ is non-permissible, so it is extraneous. Check $x = 3$: $\dfrac{9}{6} = \dfrac{9}{6}$ ✓.

m301-8-3-c.title: Connecting Graphs and Rational Equations, Part 3: Solving Graphically

cues.prompt: The equation $\dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3} = 0$ has the related function $y = \dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}$. What does its graph show?
choices: An $x$-intercept at $3$ and a hole at $(-3, 0)$, so $x = 3$
An $x$-intercept at $-3$ and a hole at $(3, 0)$, so $x = \pm 3$
An $x$-intercept at $-3$ and a hole at $(3, 6)$, so $x = -3$
cues.working: $y = \dfrac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{x - 3} = x + 3$, $x \ne 3$: a line with a hole at $(3, 6)$. It crosses the $x$-axis only at $x = -3$; the root $x = 3$ is extraneous.

m301-8-3-d.title: Connecting Graphs and Rational Equations, Part 4: Sharing a Job

cues.prompt: Working alone, Ava takes $8$ h longer than Ben to paint a fence. Together they take $3$ h. If Ben takes $t$ hours alone, which equation models the situation?
cues.working: Ben does $\dfrac{1}{t}$ of the job each hour, Ava $\dfrac{1}{t + 8}$, and together $\dfrac{1}{3}$. Solving gives $t^2 + 2t - 24 = 0$, so $t = 4$ (Ben takes $4$ h, Ava $12$ h); $t = -6$ is rejected.

cues.prompt: For $f(x) = x^2 - 1$ and $g(x) = 2x + 5$, find $(fg)(-2)$.

m301-8-4-c.title: Sums, Differences, Products and Quotients of Functions, Part 3: The Domain of a Combined Function

cues.prompt: Let $f(x) = \sqrt{x + 2}$ and $g(x) = x - 3$. What is the domain of $\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)(x)$?
cues.working: $f$ needs $x + 2 \ge 0$, so $x \ge -2$. The denominator $g(x) = x - 3$ is $0$ at $x = 3$, so $3$ is excluded too.

m301-8-5.title: Composite Functions, Part 1: A Function of a Function

cues.prompt: For $f(x) = 2x - 5$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 1$, evaluate $g(f(3))$.
cues.working: Inside first: $f(3) = 6 - 5 = 1$. Then $g(1) = 1 + 1 = 2$.

m301-8-5-b.title: Composite Functions, Part 2: From Tables and Graphs

cues.working: Inside first: $g(1) = 3$. Then $f(3) = 4$, so $f(g(1)) = 4$.

cues.prompt: For $f(x) = x^2 - 1$ and $g(x) = x + 3$, write $f(g(x))$.

m301-8-5-d.title: Composite Functions, Part 4: The Domain of a Composite Function

cues.prompt: Let $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ and $g(x) = x + 5$. What is the domain of $f(g(x))$?
cues.working: $f(g(x)) = \sqrt{x + 5}$. The input of $f$ must not be negative: $x + 5 \ge 0$, so $x \ge -5$.

m301-8-5-e.title: Composite Functions, Part 5: Decomposing a Function

cues.prompt: Write $h(x) = \sqrt{5x - 1} + 4$ as $f(g(x))$.
cues.working: First $5x - 1$ is calculated, so $g(x) = 5x - 1$. Then the square root is taken and $4$ is added, so $f(x) = \sqrt{x} + 4$. Check: $f(g(x)) = \sqrt{5x - 1} + 4$ ✓

m301-9-1.title: The Fundamental Counting Principle, Part 1: Tree Diagrams and Multiplying Choices

cues.prompt: A café makes drinks in 4 sizes, with 3 flavours and 2 kinds of milk. Each drink has one size, one flavour and one kind of milk. How many different drinks are possible?
cues.working: A drink is a size **and** a flavour **and** a kind of milk: $4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24$.

m301-9-1-b.title: The Fundamental Counting Principle, Part 2: Repetition and Restricted Boxes

cues.prompt: How many 3-digit numbers have no repeated digits?
cues.working: First digit: 1 to 9, so $9$ choices. Second: any digit except the first (0 is allowed now), so $9$. Third: $8$. So $9 \times 9 \times 8 = 648$.

m301-9-1-c.title: The Fundamental Counting Principle, Part 3: Counting in Cases

cues.prompt: From a school, 3 trails lead directly to a lake. There are also 2 trails from the school to a lookout, and 5 trails from the lookout to the lake. How many routes go from the school to the lake?
cues.working: Through the lookout: $2 \times 5 = 10$ routes ("and"). Directly: $3$ routes. Directly **or** through the lookout: $3 + 10 = 13$.

cues.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{9!}{7!}$.
cues.working: $9! = 9 \times 8 \times 7!$, so $\dfrac{9 \times 8 \times 7!}{7!} = 9 \times 8 = 72$.

m301-9-2-b.title: Permutations, Part 2: Permutations of n Objects Taken r at a Time

cues.prompt: A club of 9 members elects a president, a vice-president and a treasurer. No member can hold two positions. In how many ways can the three positions be filled?
cues.working: The positions are different, so order matters: ${}_{9}P_{3} = \dfrac{9!}{6!} = 9 \times 8 \times 7 = 504$.

m301-9-2-c.title: Permutations, Part 3: Arrangements with Identical Objects

cues.prompt: How many different arrangements are there of the letters of the word CANADA?
cues.working: 6 letters, with A appearing 3 times: $\dfrac{6!}{3!} = \dfrac{720}{6} = 120$.

cues.prompt: Five people, including Ava and Ben, stand in a line for a photo. In how many ways can they stand with Ava and Ben **not** together?
cues.working: All: $5! = 120$. Together: the block and 3 others make 4 units, $4! = 24$, times $2!$ inside the block: $48$. Apart: $120 - 48 = 72$.

m301-9-3.title: Combinations, Part 1: When Order Does Not Matter

cues.prompt: A pizza place offers 8 toppings. How many different pizzas with exactly 3 different toppings can be made?
cues.working: The order of the toppings does not matter: ${}_{8}C_{3} = \dfrac{8 \times 7 \times 6}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = \dfrac{336}{6} = 56$.

m301-9-3-b.title: Combinations, Part 2: Card Hands and Equations

cues.prompt: How many 5-card hands from a standard 52-card deck contain exactly 3 hearts and 2 spades?
cues.working: Hearts: ${}_{13}C_{3} = 286$. Spades: ${}_{13}C_{2} = 78$. A hand needs both, so multiply: $286 \times 78 = 22\,308$.

m301-9-3-c.title: Combinations, Part 3: Exactly, At Least and At Most

cues.prompt: A 3-person team is chosen from 4 seniors and 5 juniors. How many teams have at least one senior?
cues.working: All teams: ${}_{9}C_{3} = 84$. Teams with no seniors: ${}_{5}C_{3} = 10$. At least one senior: $84 - 10 = 74$.

m301-9-4.title: The Binomial Theorem, Part 1: Pascal’s Triangle

cues.prompt: The row of Pascal’s triangle that begins $1,\ 7$ is $1,\ 7,\ 21,\ 35,\ 35,\ 21,\ 7,\ 1$. What is the 5th number in the row that begins $1,\ 8$?
cues.working: Add neighbours: $1,\ 8,\ 28,\ 56,\ 70,\ \ldots$ The 5th number is $35 + 35 = 70$.

m301-9-4-b.title: The Binomial Theorem, Part 2: Pascal’s Triangle and Combinations

cues.prompt: What is the 3rd number in the row of Pascal’s triangle that begins $1,\ 10$?
