m302-1-1.title: Sets and Subsets, Part 1: Sets and Elements

chapters.title: Three ways to describe a set

cues.prompt: Let $D$ be the set of even numbers between 1 and 15. Find $n(D)$.

m302-1-1-b.title: Sets and Subsets, Part 2: Set-Builder Notation

cues.prompt: List the elements of $\{x \mid -2 < x \le 2,\ x \in I\}$.
cues.working: $-2 < x$ leaves out $-2$, and $x \le 2$ includes $2$. The integers between are $-1, 0, 1, 2$.

m302-1-1-c.title: Sets and Subsets, Part 3: Finite, Infinite and Empty Sets

cues.prompt: Which set is empty?
choices: the set of even prime numbers
the set of natural numbers less than $1$
cues.working: The natural numbers start at $1$, so none of them is less than $1$. The other sets contain $0$, $2$ and $6, 7, 8, \ldots$

m302-1-1-d.title: Sets and Subsets, Part 4: The Universal Set and Subsets

cues.prompt: Let $U = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 10\}$, $P = \{2, 3, 5, 7\}$ and $Q = \{3, 5\}$. Which statement is true?
cues.working: Both elements of $Q$, $3$ and $5$, are in $P$, so $Q \subset P$. But $2 \in P$ and $2 \notin Q$, so $P$ is not a subset of $Q$.

m302-1-1-e.title: Sets and Subsets, Part 5: Counting Subsets

cues.prompt: A pizza shop offers 4 toppings. A pizza can have any number of them, from none to all 4. How many different choices of toppings are there?
cues.working: Each topping is on or off: $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 2^4 = 16$, counting the plain pizza and the pizza with all four.

m302-1-2.title: Venn Diagrams and Set Operations, Part 1: Union and Intersection

cues.working: The intersection holds the elements in **both** sets. Only 2 and 4 are in $P$ and in $Q$.

m302-1-2-b.title: Venn Diagrams and Set Operations, Part 2: Complement and Difference

cues.working: $Q \setminus P$ is in $Q$ but not in $P$: remove $2$ and $4$ from $Q$, leaving $\{6, 8, 10\}$.

m302-1-2-c.title: Venn Diagrams and Set Operations, Part 3: Counting with Two Sets

cues.prompt: In a class of 30 students, 17 have a dog, 12 have a cat and 5 have both. How many students have neither a dog nor a cat?
cues.working: $n(D \cup C) = 17 + 12 - 5 = 24$, so $30 - 24 = 6$ have neither.

m302-1-2-d.title: Venn Diagrams and Set Operations, Part 4: Three Sets

cues.prompt: Of 50 students, 20 take art, 25 take music and 15 take drama. Of these, 7 take art and music, 5 take art and drama, 6 take music and drama, and 3 take all three. How many take only art?
cues.working: Art and music only: $7 - 3 = 4$. Art and drama only: $5 - 3 = 2$. Only art: $20 - 4 - 2 - 3 = 11$.

m302-1-2-e.title: Venn Diagrams and Set Operations, Part 5: Naming Shaded Regions

cues.prompt: A region of a Venn diagram is inside $B$ and inside $C$, but outside $A$. Which notation names it?
cues.working: Inside $B$ and $C$: $B \cap C$. But not in $A$: $(B \cap C) \setminus A$.

chapters.title: A true statement in a Venn diagram

cues.prompt: Which number is a counterexample to “If a number is a multiple of 3, then it is odd”?
cues.working: $6$ is a multiple of $3$ (the hypothesis is true) and $6$ is even (the conclusion is false).

cues.prompt: The statement “If a number is a multiple of 6, then it is a multiple of 3” is true. Which number is a counterexample to its **converse**?
cues.working: The converse is “If a number is a multiple of 3, then it is a multiple of 6.” $9$ is a multiple of $3$ but not of $6$.

m302-1-3-c.title: Conditional Statements, Part 3: The Inverse and the Contrapositive

cues.prompt: What is the contrapositive of “If it is snowing, then it is cold”?
choices: If it is cold, then it is snowing.
If it is not snowing, then it is not cold.
If it is snowing, then it is not cold.
If it is not cold, then it is not snowing.
cues.working: Switch the parts and negate both: “If it is not cold, then it is not snowing.”

cues.prompt: Which biconditional is true?
choices: An angle is a right angle if and only if it measures $90^\circ$.
A number is odd if and only if it is prime.
A shape is a rectangle if and only if it has four sides.
A number is positive if and only if it is greater than $1$.
cues.working: A is true both ways. B fails both ways: $9$ is odd but not prime, and $2$ is prime but not odd. C fails one way: a kite has four sides. D fails one way: $0.5$ is positive but not greater than $1$.

m302-2-1.title: The Fundamental Counting Principle, Part 1: Tree Diagrams and Organized Lists

cues.prompt: A sandwich comes on white, brown or rye bread, with a filling of ham, turkey, egg or cheese. How many different sandwiches with one bread and one filling are possible?
cues.working: Each of the 3 breads splits into 4 fillings: $3 \times 4 = 12$ branches.

m302-2-1-b.title: The Fundamental Counting Principle, Part 2: Multiplying the Choices

cues.prompt: A product code has 2 letters (A to Z) followed by 3 digits (0 to 9). Letters and digits may repeat. How many codes are possible?
cues.working: $26 \times 26 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 676 \times 1000 = 676\,000$.

m302-2-1-c.title: The Fundamental Counting Principle, Part 3: Add or Multiply?

cues.prompt: A school lunch is one meal and one juice. There are 4 hot meals, 3 cold meals and 2 kinds of juice. How many different lunches are possible?
cues.working: A meal is hot **or** cold: $4 + 3 = 7$. A lunch is a meal **and** a juice: $7 \times 2 = 14$.

m302-2-1-d.title: The Fundamental Counting Principle, Part 4: Counting What You Do Not Want

cues.prompt: A 3-digit lock code uses the digits 0 to 9, and digits may repeat. How many codes contain at least one 7?
cues.working: All codes: $10^3 = 1000$. Codes with no 7: each digit has 9 choices, $9^3 = 729$. At least one 7: $1000 - 729 = 271$.

cues.prompt: Evaluate $\dfrac{6!}{3!}$.
cues.working: $\dfrac{6!}{3!} = \dfrac{6 \times 5 \times 4 \times 3!}{3!} = 6 \times 5 \times 4 = 120$.

m302-2-2-b.title: Permutations, Part 2: Arranging Some of the Objects

cues.prompt: A club with 12 members elects a president, a vice-president and a secretary. No one may hold two jobs. In how many ways can the three jobs be filled?
cues.working: The jobs are different, so order matters: ${}_{12}P_{3} = 12 \times 11 \times 10 = 1320$.

m302-2-2-c.title: Permutations, Part 3: Choosing the Right Model

cues.prompt: A playlist plays 5 different songs, chosen from 20, in order, with no song played twice. Which expression counts the playlists?
cues.working: Order matters, no song repeats, and only 5 of the 20 songs are used: ${}_{20}P_{5} = 20 \times 19 \times 18 \times 17 \times 16$.

cues.prompt: There are 56 ways to award a first prize and a second prize to the people in a contest. How many people entered?
cues.working: $n(n - 1) = 56$, and $8 \times 7 = 56$, so $n = 8$. (The other root, $n = -7$, is rejected.)

m302-2-3.title: Permutations with Repetition and Restrictions, Part 1: Identical Objects

cues.prompt: How many different arrangements of the letters in the word LETTER are there?
cues.working: LETTER has 6 letters, with two E’s and two T’s: $\dfrac{6!}{2!\,2!} = \dfrac{720}{4} = 180$.

m302-2-3-b.title: Permutations with Repetition and Restrictions, Part 2: Fixed Positions

cues.prompt: Seven students line up for a photo. Ana must stand at the left end and Ben at the right end. How many line-ups are possible?
cues.working: Ana and Ben each have 1 spot. The other 5 students fill the middle 5 spots: $1 \times 1 \times 5! = 120$.

m302-2-3-c.title: Permutations with Repetition and Restrictions, Part 3: Together or Apart

cues.prompt: Five friends sit in a row of 5 seats. Two of them, Sam and Leo, must sit together. How many seatings are possible?
cues.working: Sam and Leo form one unit, so there are 4 units: $4! = 24$. Inside the unit they can swap: $24 \times 2 = 48$.

m302-2-3-d.title: Permutations with Repetition and Restrictions, Part 4: Alternating Patterns

cues.prompt: Four adults and four children sit in a row of 8 seats, alternating adult and child. How many seatings are possible?
cues.working: Two patterns (start with an adult or a child). Each: $4! \times 4! = 24 \times 24 = 576$. Total: $2 \times 576 = 1152$.

cues.prompt: Which situation is a combination?
choices: Choosing a captain and an assistant captain
cues.working: Swapping two committee members gives the same committee, so order does not matter. Swapping in the other three changes the result.

cues.prompt: A teacher chooses 4 of 10 students to present on the first day. The order of the presentations does not matter. How many groups are possible?
cues.working: ${}_{10}C_{4} = \dfrac{10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7}{4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1} = \dfrac{5040}{24} = 210$.

m302-2-4-c.title: Combinations, Part 3: Choosing from Several Groups

cues.prompt: A committee needs 2 of 5 teachers and 2 of 8 students. How many committees are possible?
A committee of 3 is chosen from 6 students and 4 teachers. How many committees include at least one teacher?
cues.working: All committees: ${}_{10}C_{3} = 120$. No teachers: ${}_{6}C_{3} = 20$. At least one teacher: $120 - 20 = 100$.

m302-3-1.title: Odds and Probability, Part 1: Odds in Favour and Against

cues.prompt: A spinner has 8 equal sections: 3 are green and 5 are yellow. What are the odds in favour of landing on green?
cues.working: Favourable: 3 green sections. Unfavourable: 5 yellow sections. The odds in favour of green are $3 : 5$.

m302-3-1-b.title: Odds and Probability, Part 2: Converting Odds and Probability

cues.prompt: The odds in favour of a team winning its next game are $4 : 7$. What is the probability that it wins?
cues.working: 4 favourable outcomes for every 7 unfavourable ones make $4 + 7 = 11$ in all, so $P(\text{win}) = \dfrac{4}{11}$.

m302-3-1-c.title: Odds and Probability, Part 3: Solving Problems with Odds

cues.prompt: A bag holds 40 tiles. The odds in favour of drawing a blue tile are $3 : 5$. How many blue tiles are in the bag?
cues.working: $P(\text{blue}) = \dfrac{3}{3 + 5} = \dfrac{3}{8}$, and $40 \times \dfrac{3}{8} = 15$ blue tiles.

m302-3-2.title: Probability Using Counting Methods, Part 1: Arrangements

cues.prompt: Seven runners, including Lena and Tom, are given lanes 1 to 7 at random. What is the probability that Lena gets lane 1 and Tom gets lane 2?
cues.working: All: $7! = 5040$. Favourable: $1 \times 1 \times 5! = 120$. $P = \dfrac{120}{5040} = \dfrac{1}{42}$.

m302-3-2-b.title: Probability Using Counting Methods, Part 2: Choosing Groups

cues.prompt: A bag holds 5 red and 7 blue marbles. Three marbles are drawn at random, all at once. What is the probability that all three are red?

m302-3-2-c.title: Probability Using Counting Methods, Part 3: At Least One

cues.prompt: Three students are chosen at random from 5 boys and 4 girls. What is the probability that at least one girl is chosen?
cues.working: No girls: ${}_{5}C_{3} = 10$ of ${}_{9}C_{3} = 84$, so $P(\text{none}) = \dfrac{10}{84} = \dfrac{5}{42}$ and $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - \dfrac{5}{42} = \dfrac{37}{42}$.

m302-3-3.title: Mutually Exclusive Events, Part 1: Adding Probabilities

cues.prompt: A bag holds 3 red, 5 green and 4 yellow marbles. One marble is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is red or yellow?
cues.working: No marble is both red and yellow, so $P(\text{red or yellow}) = \dfrac{3}{12} + \dfrac{4}{12} = \dfrac{7}{12}$.

m302-3-3-b.title: Mutually Exclusive Events, Part 2: Events That Overlap

chapters.title: A heart or a face card

cues.prompt: One card is drawn from a standard deck of 52. What is the probability that it is a king or a club?
cues.working: $P(\text{king or club}) = \dfrac{4}{52} + \dfrac{13}{52} - \dfrac{1}{52} = \dfrac{16}{52} = \dfrac{4}{13}$. The king of clubs is in both events.

m302-3-3-c.title: Mutually Exclusive Events, Part 3: Both, and Neither

cues.prompt: For a student in a class, $P(\text{cat}) = 0.4$, $P(\text{dog}) = 0.5$ and $P(\text{cat and dog}) = 0.2$. What is the probability that a student has neither pet?

m302-3-4.title: Independent and Dependent Events, Part 1: Independent Events

cues.prompt: A spinner has 4 equal sections, and one of them is red. It is spun 3 times. What is the probability that it lands on red at least once?
cues.working: $P(\text{not red}) = \dfrac{3}{4}$, so $P(\text{no red}) = \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^3 = \dfrac{27}{64}$ and $P(\text{at least one red}) = 1 - \dfrac{27}{64} = \dfrac{37}{64}$.

m302-3-4-b.title: Independent and Dependent Events, Part 2: Dependent Events

cues.prompt: A box holds 4 green and 6 yellow pens. Two pens are taken at random, without replacement. What is the probability that both are green?
cues.working: $P(\text{both green}) = \dfrac{4}{10} \times \dfrac{3}{9} = \dfrac{12}{90} = \dfrac{2}{15}$.

m302-3-4-c.title: Independent and Dependent Events, Part 3: Conditional Probability from a Table

cues.prompt: Of 120 students, 66 have no job. Of those 66, 42 are in Grade 11. Given that a student has no job, what is the probability that the student is in Grade 11?
cues.working: Use only the 66 students with no job: $P(\text{Grade 11} \mid \text{no job}) = \dfrac{42}{66} = \dfrac{7}{11}$.

m302-4-1.title: Equivalent Rational Expressions, Part 1: Non-Permissible Values

cues.prompt: What are the non-permissible values of $\dfrac{x + 3}{x^2 - 9}$?
Simplify $\dfrac{x^2 - 49}{2x - 14}$.
cues.working: $\dfrac{(x - 7)(x + 7)}{2(x - 7)}$, so $x \ne 7$, and dividing out $x - 7$ leaves $\dfrac{x + 7}{2}$.

m302-4-1-c.title: Equivalent Rational Expressions, Part 3: Equivalent Forms and Opposites

cues.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{3x - 12}{16 - x^2}$, where $x \ne -4, \ 4$.

m302-4-2.title: Operations on Rational Expressions, Part 1: Multiplying and Dividing

cues.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{5x}{x + 2} \times \dfrac{x^2 - 4}{10x^2}$, where $x \ne -2, \ 0$.
cues.working: $\dfrac{5x}{x + 2} \times \dfrac{(x - 2)(x + 2)}{10x^2}$: divide out $x + 2$, and $\dfrac{5x}{10x^2} = \dfrac{1}{2x}$, leaving $\dfrac{x - 2}{2x}$.

m302-4-2-b.title: Operations on Rational Expressions, Part 2: Adding and Subtracting

cues.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{2}{3x} + \dfrac{1}{x^2}$, where $x \ne 0$.
cues.working: The LCD is $3x^2$: $\dfrac{2}{3x} \cdot \dfrac{x}{x} + \dfrac{1}{x^2} \cdot \dfrac{3}{3} = \dfrac{2x}{3x^2} + \dfrac{3}{3x^2} = \dfrac{2x + 3}{3x^2}$.

m302-4-2-c.title: Operations on Rational Expressions, Part 3: Binomial Denominators

cues.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{3}{x - 1} + \dfrac{2}{x + 4}$, where $x \ne -4, \ 1$.

m302-4-3.title: Rational Equations, Part 1: Clearing the Fractions

cues.prompt: Solve $\dfrac{5}{x} - \dfrac{1}{3x} = \dfrac{7}{6}$.
cues.working: $x \ne 0$. Multiply every term by $6x$: $30 - 2 = 7x$, so $x = 4$. Check: $\dfrac{5}{4} - \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{14}{12} = \dfrac{7}{6}$ ✓

cues.prompt: Solve $\dfrac{x^2}{x - 2} = \dfrac{4}{x - 2}$.
cues.working: $x \ne 2$. Multiply by $x - 2$: $x^2 = 4$, so $x = \pm 2$. $x = 2$ is non-permissible, so it is extraneous. Check $x = -2$: $\dfrac{4}{-4} = -1 = \dfrac{4}{-4}$ ✓

cues.prompt: One pump can empty a flooded basement in 4 h, and a second pump can empty it in 12 h. How long do the two pumps take together?
cues.working: $\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{1}{t}$. Multiply by $12t$: $3t + t = 12$, so $t = 3$ h.

m302-4-3-d.title: Rational Equations, Part 4: Travel and Average Cost

cues.prompt: A boat travels 36 km downstream in the same time it travels 24 km upstream. The current adds 3 km/h to its speed going downstream and takes 3 km/h away going upstream. What is the boat’s speed in still water?

m302-5-1.title: Characteristics of Polynomial Functions, Part 1: Degree and Leading Coefficient

cues.prompt: State the degree, the leading coefficient and the constant term of $y = 6 + 4x^2 - x^3$.
cues.working: From the highest power down, $y = -x^3 + 4x^2 + 6$. The degree is $3$, the coefficient of $-x^3$ is $-1$, and the constant term is $6$.

m302-5-1-b.title: Characteristics of Polynomial Functions, Part 2: End Behaviour

cues.prompt: Describe the end behaviour of $y = 5 - 2x + 3x^2$.
cues.working: The leading term is $3x^2$. The degree is even, so both ends go the same way, and the leading coefficient $3$ is positive, so both ends go up.

m302-5-1-c.title: Characteristics of Polynomial Functions, Part 3: Intercepts and Turning Points

cues.prompt: Find the $x$-intercepts and the $y$-intercept of $y = (x - 2)(x + 1)(x + 4)$.
cues.working: Each factor is zero when $x = 2$, $x = -1$ or $x = -4$. At $x = 0$: $(0 - 2)(0 + 1)(0 + 4) = -8$.

m302-5-1-d.title: Characteristics of Polynomial Functions, Part 4: Domain, Range and Matching Graphs

cues.prompt: State the range of $y = 2(x + 3)^2 - 5$.
cues.working: The vertex is $(-3, -5)$ and $a = 2 > 0$, so the parabola opens up and $-5$ is its minimum value.

m302-5-2.title: Modelling Data with Polynomial Functions, Part 1: Choosing a Type of Model

cues.prompt: A scatter plot of a shop’s weekly sales rises, then falls, then rises again. Which type of regression suits the data?
choices: Linear, because the sales end higher than they start
cues.working: The pattern changes direction twice (up, down, up), so it has two turning points: a cubic model.

m302-5-2-b.title: Modelling Data with Polynomial Functions, Part 2: Interpolating and Extrapolating

cues.prompt: Data for $x$ from $10$ to $50$ give the linear model $y = 2.5x + 12$. Estimate $y$ when $x = 30$. Is this interpolation or extrapolation?
cues.working: $y = 2.5(30) + 12 = 75 + 12 = 87$. Since $30$ is between $10$ and $50$, inside the data, this is interpolation.

m302-5-2-c.title: Modelling Data with Polynomial Functions, Part 3: Using Quadratic and Cubic Models

cues.prompt: A ball’s height, in metres, $x$ seconds after it is thrown is modelled by $y = -4.9x^2 + 19.6x + 2$. When does it reach its maximum height, and what is that height?

m302-5-2-d.title: Modelling Data with Polynomial Functions, Part 4: Is the Prediction Reasonable?

chapters.title: Only the data it came from

cues.prompt: A model for the number of fish in a pond, from data for years $0$ to $6$, is $y = -15x^2 + 90x + 400$. For year $10$ it gives $y = -200$. What does this tell you?
choices: The prediction is not reasonable: year 10 is far outside the data.
The pond will have 200 fewer fish than at the start.
The model must be wrong for years 0 to 6 as well.
The prediction is reasonable, because the model fits the data.
cues.working: A pond cannot hold a negative number of fish. Year $10$ is outside the data (years $0$ to $6$), so this extrapolation uses the model where it does not apply.

m302-6-1.title: Exponential Functions, Part 1: Growth or Decay

cues.prompt: Which function shows exponential decay?
cues.working: Only $y = 6(0.9)^x$ has a base between $0$ and $1$. The other bases, $2.5$, $1.2$ and $1.1$, are greater than $1$, so those functions show growth.

m302-6-1-b.title: Exponential Functions, Part 2: Features of the Graph

cues.prompt: State the range of $y = 5(3)^x$.
cues.working: Every $y$-value is positive, and the graph approaches the asymptote $y = 0$ without reaching it. Values less than $5$ occur when $x < 0$, for example $y = 5(3)^{-1} = \frac{5}{3}$.

m302-6-1-c.title: Exponential Functions, Part 3: Finding the Equation from a Table or a Graph

cues.prompt: An exponential function has $y = 80, 40, 20, 10$ at $x = 0, 1, 2, 3$. Which equation fits?

m302-6-1-d.title: Exponential Functions, Part 4: Exponential Models in Context

cues.prompt: A town’s population is modelled by $P = 12\,000(1.03)^t$, where $t$ is the number of years from now. Which statement is true?
choices: The population grows by 103% each year.
The population starts at 12,000 and grows by 3% each year.
The population falls by 3% each year.
The population grows by 1.03 people each year.
cues.working: $1.03 = 1 + 0.03$, so the population is multiplied by $1.03$ each year: growth of 3%. The initial value is $12\,000$.

m302-6-2.title: Solving Exponential Equations, Part 1: Equations with a Common Base

m302-6-2-b.title: Solving Exponential Equations, Part 2: Reciprocals and Coefficients

cues.prompt: Solve $3\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x} = 24$.

m302-6-2-c.title: Solving Exponential Equations, Part 3: Solving with Logarithms

chapters.title: Take the log of both sides

cues.prompt: Solve $6^{x} = 40$ to the nearest hundredth.
cues.working: $x\log 6 = \log 40$, so $x = \dfrac{\log 40}{\log 6} = \dfrac{1.60206\ldots}{0.77815\ldots} \approx 2.06$. Check: $6^2 = 36$, a little less than $40$.

m302-6-2-d.title: Solving Exponential Equations, Part 4: An Expression in the Exponent

cues.prompt: Solve $3^{2x - 1} = 50$ to the nearest hundredth.
cues.working: $(2x - 1)\log 3 = \log 50$, so $2x - 1 = \dfrac{\log 50}{\log 3} = 3.5609\ldots$, $2x = 4.5609\ldots$ and $x = 2.2804\ldots \approx 2.28$.

m302-6-3.title: Logarithms and the Laws of Logarithms, Part 1: What a Logarithm Is

cues.prompt: Evaluate $\log_2 \frac{1}{8}$.

m302-6-3-b.title: Logarithms and the Laws of Logarithms, Part 2: Estimating, Change of Base and Solving

cues.prompt: Solve $\log_x 81 = 4$.
cues.working: In exponential form, $x^4 = 81$. Since $3^4 = 81$, $x = 3$.

m302-6-3-c.title: Logarithms and the Laws of Logarithms, Part 3: The Laws of Logarithms

cues.prompt: Evaluate $\log_3 6 + \log_3 4.5$.
cues.working: Product law: $\log_3 (6 \times 4.5) = \log_3 27 = 3$, because $3^3 = 27$.

m302-6-3-d.title: Logarithms and the Laws of Logarithms, Part 4: Combining, Expanding and Solving

cues.prompt: Solve $\log_2 x + \log_2 5 = 4$.
cues.working: Product law: $\log_2 5x = 4$, so $5x = 2^4 = 16$ and $x = \frac{16}{5}$, which is positive.

m302-6-4.title: Modelling with Exponential and Logarithmic Functions, Part 1: Compound Interest

cues.prompt: \$2000 is invested at 6% per year, compounded quarterly, for 5 years. Which expression gives the final amount, in dollars?
cues.working: Quarterly is 4 times a year: $i = \dfrac{0.06}{4} = 0.015$ and $n = 4 \times 5 = 20$. So $A = 2000(1.015)^{20} \approx 2693.71$.

m302-6-4-b.title: Modelling with Exponential and Logarithmic Functions, Part 2: Growth, Depreciation and Half-Life

cues.prompt: A 200 mg sample has a half-life of 5 days, so $A = 200\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/5}$. How much remains after 15 days?
cues.working: $\dfrac{t}{h} = \dfrac{15}{5} = 3$ half-lives, so $A = 200\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{200}{8} = 25$ mg.

m302-6-4-c.title: Modelling with Exponential and Logarithmic Functions, Part 3: Using a Regression Equation

cues.prompt: A town’s population is modelled by $y = 4500(1.025)^x$, where $x$ is the number of years since the data began. The data cover 10 years. Estimate the population at $x = 4$, and say whether this is interpolation or extrapolation.
cues.working: $y = 4500(1.025)^4 = 4500(1.10381\ldots) = 4967.15\ldots$, about $4967$. Since $4$ is inside the $10$ years of data, this is interpolation.

m302-6-4-d.title: Modelling with Exponential and Logarithmic Functions, Part 4: Logarithmic Scales

cues.prompt: Using $\dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = 10^{M_1 - M_2}$, how many times as intense is a magnitude 7.2 earthquake as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake?

m302-7-1.title: Periodic Behaviour and Sinusoidal Functions, Part 1: Periodic Functions

cues.prompt: Which of these quantities is periodic?
choices: The temperature of a cup of tea as it cools
The height of the tip of a fan blade spinning at a steady speed
The height of a ball that bounces a little lower each time
The amount of money in a savings account that earns interest
cues.working: The fan blade turns at a steady speed, so its tip repeats exactly the same heights on every turn. Each bounce of the ball is lower than the last, so no cycle repeats exactly.

m302-7-1-b.title: Periodic Behaviour and Sinusoidal Functions, Part 2: Reading a Sinusoidal Graph

cues.prompt: A sinusoidal graph has a maximum value of $10$ and a minimum value of $-2$. What are its midline and amplitude?

m302-7-1-c.title: Periodic Behaviour and Sinusoidal Functions, Part 3: Features from the Equation

cues.prompt: For $y = -5\sin(4x) + 2$, with $x$ in degrees, which statement is correct?
cues.working: Amplitude $|{-5}| = 5$; period $\dfrac{360^\circ}{4} = 90^\circ$; midline $y = 2$, so the range runs from $2 - 5 = -3$ to $2 + 5 = 7$.

m302-7-1-d.title: Periodic Behaviour and Sinusoidal Functions, Part 4: The Period in Degrees and Radians

cues.prompt: With $x$ in radians, what is the period of $y = 5\cos(6x) + 1$?
cues.working: The period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b} = \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$. A larger $b$ gives a shorter period, so the answer must be less than $2\pi$.

m302-7-1-e.title: Periodic Behaviour and Sinusoidal Functions, Part 5: Sinusoidal Situations

cues.prompt: A Ferris wheel has a diameter of $30$ m. Riders board $3$ m above the ground, and one rotation takes $80$ s. What is the midline of a rider’s height?
cues.working: The radius is $15$ m, so the centre of the wheel is $3 + 15 = 18$ m above the ground. Check: the maximum is $3 + 30 = 33$ and $\dfrac{33 + 3}{2} = 18$.

m302-7-2.title: Modelling Data with Sinusoidal Functions, Part 1: Reading a Regression Equation

cues.prompt: A model of the average temperature in a city in month $m$ is $T(m) = 11.2\sin(0.524m - 1.83) + 3.4$, in °C. What are the highest temperature and the period?
cues.working: Maximum $= d + a = 3.4 + 11.2 = 14.6$. Period $= \dfrac{2\pi}{0.524} = 11.99\ldots \approx 12$ months: one year.

m302-7-2-b.title: Modelling Data with Sinusoidal Functions, Part 2: Making Predictions in Radian Mode

cues.prompt: Use $L(n) = 5.07\sin(0.0172n - 1.39) + 12.16$ to estimate the hours of daylight on day $200$.

m302-7-2-c.title: Modelling Data with Sinusoidal Functions, Part 3: Interpolating and Extrapolating

cues.prompt: The model $h(t) = 2.85\sin(0.506t - 1.21) + 4.62$ was made from data for $0 \le t \le 24$ hours after midnight. Estimate the water level at 10:00 p.m. Is this interpolation or extrapolation?

m302-7-2-d.title: Modelling Data with Sinusoidal Functions, Part 4: When Is the Maximum?

cues.prompt: The water level at a dock is $h(t) = 2.85\sin(0.506t - 1.21) + 4.62$, in metres, $t$ hours after midnight. When is the first high tide after midnight?
cues.working: High tide is the maximum: $0.506t - 1.21 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $t = \dfrac{\pi/2 + 1.21}{0.506} = 5.49\ldots \approx 5.50$, about 5:30 a.m.

m302-8-1.title: Puzzles and Games, Part 1: Problem-Solving Strategies

cues.prompt: I am a two-digit number. The sum of my digits is $9$, and my ones digit is $5$ more than my tens digit. What number am I?
cues.working: The two-digit numbers with a digit sum of $9$ are $18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72, 81$ and $90$. Only $27$ has a ones digit $5$ more than its tens digit: $7 = 2 + 5$.

m302-8-1-b.title: Puzzles and Games, Part 2: Magic Squares

cues.prompt: In a 3 by 3 magic square, the top row is $4$, $9$ and $8$, and the centre is $7$. What number goes in the bottom-right corner?
cues.working: The magic sum is $4 + 9 + 8 = 21$. The bottom-right corner is on the diagonal through the top-left corner and the centre: $4 + 7 + x = 21$, so $x = 10$.

cues.prompt: In a 4 by 4 Sudoku, row 2 contains $3$ and $1$, and its two empty cells are A2 and D2. Column D already contains a $2$. What digit goes in D2?
cues.working: Row 2 is missing $2$ and $4$. Column D already has a $2$, so D2 cannot be $2$: D2 $= 4$ (and then A2 $= 2$).

m302-8-1-d.title: Puzzles and Games, Part 4: Logic Puzzles

cues.prompt: Dev, Emma and Farah each own a different pet: a cat, a dog or a fish. Emma does not own the dog or the fish. Farah does not own the dog. Who owns the fish?
cues.working: Emma owns neither the dog nor the fish, so Emma owns the cat. The dog is not Emma’s or Farah’s, so Dev owns the dog. That leaves the fish for Farah.

m302-8-1-e.title: Puzzles and Games, Part 5: Finding a Winning Strategy

cues.prompt: In the same game (take $1$, $2$ or $3$ counters; whoever takes the last counter wins), the pile starts with $22$ counters. How many should the first player take?
cues.working: $22 = 20 + 2$, and $20$ is a multiple of $4$. Take $2$ to leave $20$, then make each round total $4$.

m302-8-1-f.title: Puzzles and Games, Part 6: A Systematic Search

cues.prompt: Start with an empty 3 L jug and an empty 5 L jug. Fill the 3 L jug and pour it into the 5 L jug. Fill the 3 L jug again, and pour it into the 5 L jug until the 5 L jug is full. How much water is left in the 3 L jug?
cues.working: The states are $(3, 0)$, $(0, 3)$, $(3, 3)$, $(1, 5)$. The 5 L jug had room for only $2$ L more, so $3 - 2 = 1$ L is left.

m302-8-2.title: The Mathematics Research Project, Part 1: Choosing a Research Question

cues.prompt: Which research question is best?
choices: What do people think of trucks?
For used pickup trucks advertised on one website this month, how is the asking price related to the age of the truck?
How has the value of every vehicle in the world changed since cars were invented?
cues.working: It is specific (used pickup trucks on one website this month), measurable (price and age are numbers) and realistic (the listings can be collected in a few hours).

m302-8-2-b.title: The Mathematics Research Project, Part 2: Collecting Data

cues.prompt: A student uses a table of average monthly temperatures from a national weather service’s website. What kind of data is this?
cues.working: The weather service collected the data, not the student, so they are secondary. Temperatures are numbers, so they are quantitative.

m302-8-2-c.title: The Mathematics Research Project, Part 3: Spotting Bias

cues.prompt: A survey asks: “Do you agree that our excellent mayor deserves a second term?” What kind of bias is most likely?
cues.working: Calling the mayor “excellent” pushes people toward agreeing: the wording of the question biases the answers.

m302-8-2-d.title: The Mathematics Research Project, Part 4: Choosing Graphs and Averages

cues.prompt: The times, in minutes, that seven students take to get to school are $8$, $10$, $11$, $12$, $14$, $15$ and $75$. Which value best represents a typical time?
cues.working: The mean is $\dfrac{145}{7} \approx 20.7$, longer than six of the seven times, because the outlier $75$ pulls it up. The median, the 4th of the 7 ordered times, is $12$.

m302-8-2-e.title: The Mathematics Research Project, Part 5: Evaluating Claims

cues.prompt: A poll finds that $41\%$ of voters support a plan, with a margin of error of $3$ percentage points, $19$ times out of $20$. Which range likely contains the percent for all voters?
cues.working: A margin of error of $3$ percentage points goes both ways: $41 - 3 = 38$ and $41 + 3 = 44$.

m302-8-2-f.title: The Mathematics Research Project, Part 6: Misleading Graphs

cues.prompt: The vertical axis of a bar graph starts at $40$. The bars show $45$ and $50$. How many times as tall does the second bar look, and what is the actual percent increase?
cues.working: Above the axis, the bars show $50 - 40 = 10$ and $45 - 40 = 5$, so the second looks $2$ times as tall. The actual increase is $\dfrac{50 - 45}{45} \times 100 \approx 11.1\%$.

m303-1-1.title: Precision and Accuracy, Part 1: The Precision of an Instrument

cues.prompt: A tape measure has $8$ equal spaces between each pair of inch marks. What is its precision?
cues.working: Eight equal spaces fill one inch, so each space, the smallest unit, is $\tfrac{1}{8}$ in.

m303-1-1-b.title: Precision and Accuracy, Part 2: The Precision of a Measurement

cues.prompt: Which measurement is the most precise?
cues.working: $12.46\text{ cm}$ is to the nearest $0.01\text{ cm} = 0.1\text{ mm}$. The others are to the nearest $1\text{ mm}$, $10\text{ mm}$ and $1\text{ mm}$.

cues.prompt: A gauge block is exactly $50.00\text{ mm}$ long. Which reading of it is the most accurate?
cues.working: The differences from $50.00$ are $0.02$, $0.05$, $0.1$ and $0.1\text{ mm}$. The smallest difference, $0.02\text{ mm}$, is the most accurate.

m303-1-1-d.title: Precision and Accuracy, Part 4: Percent Error

cues.prompt: A test mass of exactly $250\text{ g}$ reads $252\text{ g}$ on a scale. What is the percent error?
A digital scale shows grams to one decimal place, and a bag of flour reads $452.3\text{ g}$. Between what values is its true mass?
cues.working: The smallest unit is $0.1\text{ g}$, so the uncertainty is $\pm 0.05\text{ g}$: $452.3 - 0.05 = 452.25$ and $452.3 + 0.05 = 452.35$.

cues.prompt: A pipe must be $150 \pm 2\text{ mm}$ long. Which length is **not** acceptable?
cues.working: Least: $150 - 2 = 148\text{ mm}$. Greatest: $150 + 2 = 152\text{ mm}$. Only $152.4\text{ mm}$ is outside the limits: it is too long.

m303-1-2-c.title: Uncertainty and Tolerance, Part 3: Unequal and Percent Tolerances

cues.prompt: A bag of fertilizer is labelled $20\text{ kg}$, with a tolerance of $\pm 2\%$. What is the least acceptable mass?
cues.working: $2\%$ of $20$ is $0.02 \times 20 = 0.4\text{ kg}$, so the least mass is $20 - 0.4 = 19.6\text{ kg}$.

m303-1-2-d.title: Uncertainty and Tolerance, Part 4: Tolerance Stacking and Clearance

cues.prompt: Two blocks, $45.0 \pm 0.2\text{ mm}$ and $30.0 \pm 0.1\text{ mm}$, are placed end to end. What is the greatest possible total length?
cues.working: Nominal total: $45.0 + 30.0 = 75.0\text{ mm}$. Tolerances add: $0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3\text{ mm}$. Greatest: $75.0 + 0.3 = 75.3\text{ mm}$.

m303-2-1.title: The Sine Law, Part 1: Oblique Triangles and Matching Pairs

cues.prompt: In $\triangle PQR$, $\angle P = 40^\circ$, $\angle Q = 75^\circ$ and $\angle R = 65^\circ$. Which side is the longest?
choices: You cannot tell without a side length.
cues.working: The largest angle is $\angle Q = 75^\circ$, so the longest side is the one across from it: side $q$.

m303-2-1-b.title: The Sine Law, Part 2: The Law and Why It Works

cues.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle A = 50^\circ$, $\angle B = 65^\circ$ and $a = 12\text{ cm}$. Which equation can find side $b$?
cues.working: Side $a = 12$ pairs with $\angle A = 50^\circ$, and side $b$ pairs with $\angle B = 65^\circ$. With the sides on top, $\dfrac{b}{\sin 65^\circ} = \dfrac{12}{\sin 50^\circ}$.

m303-2-1-c.title: The Sine Law, Part 3: Finding a Side

cues.prompt: In $\triangle XYZ$, $\angle X = 35^\circ$, $\angle Y = 80^\circ$ and $x = 9.0\text{ m}$. Find side $y$, to the nearest tenth of a metre.
cues.working: $\dfrac{y}{\sin 80^\circ} = \dfrac{9.0}{\sin 35^\circ}$, so $y = \dfrac{9.0\sin 80^\circ}{\sin 35^\circ} \approx 15.5\text{ m}$.

m303-2-1-d.title: The Sine Law, Part 4: Finding an Angle

chapters.title: Why there is only one answer

cues.prompt: In $\triangle ABC$, $a = 10\text{ cm}$, $b = 7\text{ cm}$ and $\angle A = 80^\circ$. Find $\angle B$, to the nearest tenth of a degree.
cues.working: $\sin B = \dfrac{7\sin 80^\circ}{10} \approx 0.6894$, so $\angle B = \sin^{-1}(0.6894) \approx 43.6^\circ$.

m303-2-2.title: The Cosine Law, Part 1: Finding a Side

cues.prompt: In $\triangle PQR$, $q = 7\text{ m}$, $r = 10\text{ m}$ and $\angle P = 40^\circ$. Find side $p$, to the nearest tenth of a metre.

m303-2-2-b.title: The Cosine Law, Part 2: An Obtuse Contained Angle

chapters.title: A wider angle, a longer side

cues.prompt: In $\triangle DEF$, $d = 5\text{ cm}$, $e = 8\text{ cm}$ and $\angle F = 130^\circ$. Find side $f$, to the nearest tenth of a centimetre.

m303-2-2-c.title: The Cosine Law, Part 3: Finding an Angle

cues.prompt: A triangle has sides of $5\text{ m}$, $7\text{ m}$ and $10\text{ m}$. What is its largest angle, to the nearest tenth of a degree?
cues.working: The largest angle is opposite $10\text{ m}$: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{5^2 + 7^2 - 10^2}{2(5)(7)} = \dfrac{-26}{70} \approx -0.3714$, so $\theta \approx 111.8^\circ$.

m303-2-3.title: Solving Problems with Oblique Triangles, Part 1: Choosing a Law

cues.prompt: A surveyor knows all three sides of a triangular lot: $42\text{ m}$, $55\text{ m}$ and $61\text{ m}$. Which law finds one of its angles?
cues.working: Three sides and no angles: there is no matching pair, so use the cosine law.

m303-2-3-b.title: Solving Problems with Oblique Triangles, Part 2: A Truss and Two Lookout Towers

chapters.title: The bottom chord of a truss

cues.prompt: Lookout towers $P$ and $Q$ are $20\text{ km}$ apart. A fire $F$ makes $\angle P = 48^\circ$ and $\angle Q = 57^\circ$. Which equation finds $QF$?
cues.working: $\angle F = 180^\circ - 48^\circ - 57^\circ = 75^\circ$, across from $PQ = 20$. $QF$ is across from $\angle P = 48^\circ$, so $QF \approx 15.4\text{ km}$.

m303-2-3-c.title: Solving Problems with Oblique Triangles, Part 3: Turns and Angles of Elevation

cues.prompt: A hiker walks $6\text{ km}$, turns $35^\circ$ to the left, and walks $4\text{ km}$. Which equation gives the distance $d$ back to the start?
cues.working: The inside angle is $180^\circ - 35^\circ = 145^\circ$, between the two known sides, so use the cosine law: $d \approx 9.6\text{ km}$.

m303-3-1.title: Properties of Triangles and Quadrilaterals, Part 1: Angles in Triangles

cues.prompt: An isosceles triangle has two base angles of $52^\circ$. What is the angle between its two equal sides?
cues.working: The base angles together make $52^\circ + 52^\circ = 104^\circ$, so the third angle is $180^\circ - 104^\circ = 76^\circ$.

m303-3-1-b.title: Properties of Triangles and Quadrilaterals, Part 2: The Quadrilateral Family

cues.prompt: A quadrilateral has exactly one pair of parallel sides, and its two non-parallel sides are equal. What is its most specific name?
cues.working: Exactly one pair of parallel sides makes it a trapezoid, and equal non-parallel sides make it an **isosceles** trapezoid. A parallelogram needs two pairs of parallel sides.

m303-3-1-c.title: Properties of Triangles and Quadrilaterals, Part 3: Parallelograms

cues.prompt: $PQRS$ is a parallelogram with $\angle P = 107^\circ$. What is $\angle Q$?
cues.working: $\angle Q$ is next to $\angle P$, so they add to $180^\circ$: $\angle Q = 180^\circ - 107^\circ = 73^\circ$.

m303-3-1-d.title: Properties of Triangles and Quadrilaterals, Part 4: Diagonals of Rectangles and Rhombuses

cues.prompt: $ABCD$ is a rhombus with $\angle ABC = 70^\circ$. Its diagonals meet at $E$. What is $\angle BAE$?
cues.working: Diagonal $BD$ bisects $\angle B$: $\angle ABE = 35^\circ$. The diagonals are perpendicular: $\angle AEB = 90^\circ$. So $\angle BAE = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 35^\circ = 55^\circ$.

m303-3-1-e.title: Properties of Triangles and Quadrilaterals, Part 5: Trapezoids and Kites

cues.prompt: In kite $KLMN$, $KL = KN$ and $ML = MN$. If $\angle K = 90^\circ$ and $\angle M = 56^\circ$, what is $\angle L$?
cues.working: $\angle L = \angle N$, so $2\angle L = 360^\circ - 90^\circ - 56^\circ = 214^\circ$ and $\angle L = 107^\circ$.

m303-3-2.title: Angles in Regular Polygons, Part 1: The Interior Angle Sum

cues.prompt: A convex polygon has 9 sides. What is the sum of its interior angles?
cues.working: $180^\circ(9 - 2) = 180^\circ \times 7 = 1260^\circ$. $1620^\circ$ is $180^\circ \times 9$, which forgets to subtract 2.

m303-3-2-b.title: Angles in Regular Polygons, Part 2: Interior Angles of Regular Polygons

cues.prompt: What is each interior angle of a regular decagon (10 sides)?
cues.working: Angle sum: $180^\circ(10 - 2) = 1440^\circ$. Each angle: $1440^\circ \div 10 = 144^\circ$.

m303-3-2-c.title: Angles in Regular Polygons, Part 3: Exterior Angles

cues.prompt: What is each exterior angle of a regular polygon with 12 sides?
cues.working: The exterior angles add to $360^\circ$, so each one is $360^\circ \div 12 = 30^\circ$. (Each interior angle is $180^\circ - 30^\circ = 150^\circ$.)

m303-3-2-d.title: Angles in Regular Polygons, Part 4: Finding the Number of Sides

cues.prompt: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is $165^\circ$. How many sides does it have?
cues.working: Exterior angle: $180^\circ - 165^\circ = 15^\circ$. Number of sides: $360^\circ \div 15^\circ = 24$.

m303-3-3.title: Problems with Polygons, Part 1: Perimeters and Corner Angles

cues.prompt: A table top is a regular octagon with sides of $0.4\text{ m}$. How much trim goes around its edge, and what angle is each corner?
cues.working: Perimeter: $8 \times 0.4 = 3.2\text{ m}$. Corner angle: $\dfrac{180^\circ(8 - 2)}{8} = \dfrac{1080^\circ}{8} = 135^\circ$.

m303-3-3-b.title: Problems with Polygons, Part 2: Mitre Cuts

cues.prompt: What mitre saw setting is needed for a frame shaped like a regular hexagon (6 sides)?
cues.working: Mitre angle $= \dfrac{180^\circ}{n} = \dfrac{180^\circ}{6} = 30^\circ$, half of the $60^\circ$ exterior angle.

m303-3-3-c.title: Problems with Polygons, Part 3: Central Angles

cues.prompt: A table top is a regular pentagon made of 5 identical triangular pieces that meet at the centre. What angle does each piece have at each of its outside corners?
cues.working: Central angle: $360^\circ \div 5 = 72^\circ$. Each outside angle: $\dfrac{180^\circ - 72^\circ}{2} = 54^\circ$. Check: $2 \times 54^\circ = 108^\circ$, a pentagon’s interior angle.

m303-3-3-d.title: Problems with Polygons, Part 4: Tiling with Regular Polygons

cues.prompt: Each angle of a regular 12-sided polygon is $150^\circ$. Two of them meet at a corner. Which regular polygon fills the gap that is left?
cues.working: $360^\circ - 2(150^\circ) = 60^\circ$. A regular polygon with $60^\circ$ angles is an equilateral triangle.

m303-4-1.title: Translations, Reflections and Rotations, Part 1: Translations

chapters.title: Moving a part on a cutting table

cues.prompt: The point $P(-2, 3)$ is translated 4 units right and 5 units down. Where is its image $P'$?

m303-4-1-b.title: Translations, Reflections and Rotations, Part 2: Reflections

chapters.title: A logo in a window line

cues.prompt: The point $(5, -2)$ is reflected in the horizontal line $y = 1$. Where is its image?
cues.working: The point is $1 - (-2) = 3$ units below the line, so its image is 3 units above it: $y = 1 + 3 = 4$. Rule: $2(1) - (-2) = 4$. The image is $(5, 4)$.

m303-4-1-c.title: Translations, Reflections and Rotations, Part 3: Rotations about the Origin

chapters.title: A quarter turn of a tile

cues.prompt: The point $(4, 3)$ is rotated $90^\circ$ counterclockwise about the origin. Where is its image?
cues.working: A $90^\circ$ counterclockwise turn uses $(x, y) \to (-y, x)$, so $(4, 3) \to (-3, 4)$, in quadrant II.

m303-4-1-d.title: Translations, Reflections and Rotations, Part 4: Describing a Transformation

cues.prompt: A triangle is transformed so that $A(1, 2) \to A'(2, -1)$ and $B(4, 2) \to B'(2, -4)$. Which transformation is it?
choices: A rotation of $90^\circ$ counterclockwise about the origin
A rotation of $90^\circ$ clockwise about the origin
cues.working: Both pairs follow $(x, y) \to (y, -x)$: $(1, 2) \to (2, -1)$ and $(4, 2) \to (2, -4)$. That is a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation about the origin.

m303-4-1-e.title: Translations, Reflections and Rotations, Part 5: Two Transformations in a Row

cues.prompt: The point $Q(1, 4)$ is translated 3 units right, and then the image is reflected in the $x$-axis. Where does it end up?
cues.working: Translate 3 right: $(1, 4) \to (4, 4)$. Reflect in the $x$-axis: $(4, 4) \to (4, -4)$.

m303-4-2.title: Dilations, Part 1: What a Dilation Does

cues.prompt: The point $(6, -9)$ is dilated about the origin by a scale factor of $\tfrac{1}{3}$. Where is its image?
cues.working: Multiply both coordinates by $\tfrac{1}{3}$: $\left(\tfrac{1}{3} \times 6,\ \tfrac{1}{3} \times (-9)\right) = (2, -3)$.

m303-4-2-b.title: Dilations, Part 2: Finding the Scale Factor

cues.prompt: A photo $20\text{ cm}$ wide is printed $16\text{ cm}$ wide. What is the scale factor of the print?
cues.working: $k = \dfrac{\text{image}}{\text{original}} = \dfrac{16}{20} = 0.8$. Since $0.8 < 1$, the print is a reduction.

m303-4-2-c.title: Dilations, Part 3: Perimeter and Area after a Dilation

cues.prompt: A rectangle with an area of $12\text{ m}^2$ is dilated by a scale factor of $3$. What is the area of the image?
cues.working: Area is multiplied by $k^2 = 3^2 = 9$: $9 \times 12 = 108\text{ m}^2$.

m303-4-2-d.title: Dilations, Part 4: Scale Drawings and Scale Models

cues.prompt: A plan is drawn at a scale of $1 : 100$. A room on the plan is $4\text{ cm}$ by $3\text{ cm}$. What is the real area of the room?
cues.working: Real lengths: $4 \times 100 = 400\text{ cm} = 4\text{ m}$ and $3 \times 100 = 300\text{ cm} = 3\text{ m}$. Area: $4 \times 3 = 12\text{ m}^2$.

m303-5-1.title: Patterns, Tables and Graphs, Part 1: Linear Patterns in Tables

cues.prompt: For $x = 0, 1, 2, 3$, which list of $y$-values makes a linear relation?
cues.working: In B, $y$ changes by $-3$ every time $x$ goes up by $1$, so the changes are equal: linear. In D, the changes are $3, 3, 6$.

m303-5-1-b.title: Patterns, Tables and Graphs, Part 2: Rate of Change and Initial Value

cues.prompt: A tank is being filled. At $0, 5, 10$ and $15$ minutes, it holds $120, 220, 320$ and $420$ litres. Find the rate of change and the initial value.
cues.working: The water goes up $100$ L every $5$ minutes: $\dfrac{100}{5} = 20$ L per minute. At $0$ minutes, the tank holds $120$ L.

m303-5-1-c.title: Patterns, Tables and Graphs, Part 3: Reading a Graph

cues.prompt: A graph of a gym’s total fees passes through $(0, 40)$ and $(6, 130)$, where $x$ is the number of months and $y$ is the total cost in dollars. Find the rate of change and the initial value.
cues.working: Rise: $130 - 40 = 90$. Run: $6 - 0 = 6$. Rate: $\dfrac{90}{6} = 15$ dollars per month. The line crosses the vertical axis at $40$, so the initial value is \$40.

m303-5-1-d.title: Patterns, Tables and Graphs, Part 4: Working Back to the Initial Value

cues.prompt: An electrician charges \$150 for a $2$-hour job and \$270 for a $5$-hour job. The cost is linear. What is the initial value (the call-out fee)?
cues.working: Rate: $\dfrac{270 - 150}{5 - 2} = \dfrac{120}{3} = 40$ dollars per hour. Two hours cost $2 \times 40 = 80$, so the fee is $150 - 80 = 70$ dollars.

m303-5-2.title: Writing Linear Equations, Part 1: The Equation y = mx + b

cues.prompt: A gym charges a \$49 joining fee plus \$32 per month. Which equation gives the total cost $C$, in dollars, for $n$ months?
cues.working: The \$32 is charged for each month, so it multiplies $n$: $m = 32$. The \$49 fee is charged once, at the start: $b = 49$.

m303-5-2-b.title: Writing Linear Equations, Part 2: Using an Equation

cues.prompt: A rental van costs $C = 0.35d + 59$ dollars for $d$ kilometres. How far can you drive for \$108?

m303-5-2-c.title: Writing Linear Equations, Part 3: Equations from Tables and Two Facts

cues.prompt: A candle is $24$ cm tall when it is lit. After $3$ hours, it is $16.5$ cm tall. Its height is linear. Which equation gives its height $h$, in centimetres, after $t$ hours?
cues.working: $m = \dfrac{16.5 - 24}{3 - 0} = \dfrac{-7.5}{3} = -2.5$ cm per hour, and $b = 24$, the height when lit. So $h = 24 - 2.5t$.

m303-5-2-d.title: Writing Linear Equations, Part 4: Comparing Two Offers

cues.prompt: Plan A costs \$20 a month plus \$6 per GB of data. Plan B costs \$44 a month plus \$2 per GB. For how many GB do the plans cost the same?
cues.working: $6g + 20 = 2g + 44$, so $4g = 24$ and $g = 6$. Both plans cost $6(6) + 20 = 56$ dollars.

m303-5-3.title: Interpolating and Extrapolating, Part 1: Interpolation and Extrapolation

cues.prompt: A tree’s height was measured every year from age $10$ to age $40$. Which estimate is an interpolation?
choices: Its height when planted, at age $0$
cues.working: Age $25$ is between $10$ and $40$, inside the data, so the estimate is an interpolation. The other three ages are outside the data.

m303-5-3-b.title: Interpolating and Extrapolating, Part 2: Extrapolating with the Rate or the Equation

cues.prompt: A print shop charges $C = 0.12p + 15$ dollars for $p$ pages. You have \$40. How many pages can you print?
cues.working: $40 = 0.12p + 15$, so $25 = 0.12p$ and $p \approx 208.3$. A budget means rounding down: $208$ pages cost \$39.96, but $209$ pages cost \$40.08.

m303-5-3-c.title: Interpolating and Extrapolating, Part 3: Lines of Best Fit

cues.prompt: For students who studied from $2$ to $10$ hours, the line of best fit is $s = 3.5h + 52$, where $s$ is the test score. Estimate the score for $6$ hours of study. Is this interpolation or extrapolation?
cues.working: $s = 3.5(6) + 52 = 21 + 52 = 73$. Since $6$ hours is between $2$ and $10$ hours, inside the data, this is interpolation.

m303-5-3-d.title: Interpolating and Extrapolating, Part 4: When Is Extrapolation Reasonable?

cues.prompt: A puppy gained about $0.5$ kg a week in its first $12$ weeks, from $1$ kg at birth, so $M = 0.5w + 1$. Which prediction is most reasonable?
cues.working: $14$ weeks is just past the data, so the puppy is still growing in much the same way: $0.5(14) + 1 = 8$ kg. The others go far beyond the data or give an impossible answer.

m303-6-1.title: Mean, Median and Mode, Part 1: The Mean

cues.prompt: A café sold $42, 38, 51, 45$ and $49$ muffins on five days. What is the mean number of muffins sold per day?

m303-6-1-b.title: Mean, Median and Mode, Part 2: The Median and the Mode

cues.prompt: Find the median of $14, 9, 21, 9, 17, 12$.
cues.working: In order: $9, 9, 12, 14, 17, 21$. With $6$ values, the median is halfway between the third and fourth values: $(12 + 14) \div 2 = 13$.

m303-6-1-c.title: Mean, Median and Mode, Part 3: Outliers and Choosing a Measure

cues.prompt: Five homes on a street sold for $310, 295, 320, 305$ and $1200$ thousand dollars. Which measure best describes a typical price?
cues.working: The $1200$ is an outlier. It pulls the mean up to $2430 \div 5 = 486$. In order, $295, 305, 310, 320, 1200$: the median, $310$, sits among the typical prices.

m303-6-1-d.title: Mean, Median and Mode, Part 4: Finding a Missing Value

cues.prompt: A salesperson needs a mean of at least $20$ sales a week over $4$ weeks. The first $3$ weeks had $18, 23$ and $15$ sales. How many sales are needed in week $4$?
cues.working: Total needed: $20 \times 4 = 80$. So far: $18 + 23 + 15 = 56$. Week $4$: $80 - 56 = 24$ sales.

m303-6-2.title: Weighted and Trimmed Means, Part 1: Weighted Means for Course Marks

cues.prompt: A course counts homework $40\%$ and the final exam $60\%$. A student has $90\%$ on homework and $70\%$ on the exam. What is the final mark?

m303-6-2-b.title: Weighted and Trimmed Means, Part 2: Weighted Means with Quantities

cues.prompt: A café bought $30$ kg of coffee at \$12.50 per kg and $20$ kg at \$15.00 per kg. What was the mean price per kilogram?
cues.working: Total cost: $30(12.50) + 20(15.00) = 375 + 300 = 675$ dollars, for $50$ kg. Mean price: $675 \div 50 = 13.50$ dollars per kg.

m303-6-2-c.title: Weighted and Trimmed Means, Part 3: Trimmed Means

cues.prompt: Eight judges give the scores $5, 9, 7, 8, 8, 10, 7, 9$. The highest and the lowest scores are dropped. What is the trimmed mean?

m303-6-2-d.title: Weighted and Trimmed Means, Part 4: The Mark You Need on a Final Exam

cues.prompt: Labs count $30\%$, tests $30\%$ and the final exam $40\%$. A student has $80\%$ on labs and $70\%$ on tests, and wants a final mark of $80\%$. What mark is needed on the exam?

m303-6-3.title: Percentiles, Part 1: What a Percentile Means

cues.prompt: In a wage survey, a carpenter’s wage is at the $70$th percentile. What does this mean?
choices: It is $70\%$ of the highest wage
About $30\%$ earn the same or less
About $70\%$ earn the same or less
cues.working: At the $70$th percentile, about $70\%$ of the carpenters in the survey earn the same or less, and about $30\%$ earn more.

m303-6-3-b.title: Percentiles, Part 2: The Percentile Rank Formula

cues.prompt: In a class of $25$, $16$ students scored lower than Ben, and $3$ others had the same score as Ben. What is Ben’s percentile rank?

m303-6-3-c.title: Percentiles, Part 3: The Value at a Percentile

cues.prompt: Twelve values in order: $3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18, 20$. Find the $75$th percentile.
cues.working: $R = 0.75 \times 12 = 9$, a whole number, so use the mean of the $9$th and $10$th values: $(15 + 17) \div 2 = 16$.

cues.prompt: Maya scored $68$ in a group of $25$: $18$ scored lower, and no one else had that score. Leo scored $74$ in a group of $40$: $25$ scored lower, and $1$ other had that score. Who did better compared with their own group?
cues.working: Maya: $\dfrac{18 + 0.5(1)}{25} \times 100 = 74$. Leo: $\dfrac{25 + 0.5(2)}{40} \times 100 = 65$. Maya has the higher percentile rank.

m303-7-1.title: Probability and Odds, Part 1: Probability as a Fraction, Decimal and Percent

cues.prompt: A carton of 24 eggs holds 3 cracked eggs. One egg is taken at random. What is the probability that it is cracked, as a percent?
cues.working: $\dfrac{3}{24} = \dfrac{1}{8} = 0.125 = 12.5\%$. The probability that the egg is not cracked is $1 - 0.125 = 0.875$, or $87.5\%$.

m303-7-1-b.title: Probability and Odds, Part 2: Odds in Favour and Against

cues.prompt: A bag holds 30 tiles, and 5 of them are red. One tile is drawn at random. What are the odds against drawing a red tile?
cues.working: Favourable: 5 red tiles. Unfavourable: $30 - 5 = 25$. The odds against are $25 : 5 = 5 : 1$.

m303-7-1-c.title: Probability and Odds, Part 3: Converting Odds and Probability

cues.prompt: The odds in favour of a seed sprouting are $4 : 1$. What is the probability that it sprouts, as a percent?
cues.working: 4 favourable outcomes for every 1 unfavourable one make $4 + 1 = 5$ in all, so $P(\text{sprouts}) = \dfrac{4}{5} = 80\%$.

m303-7-1-d.title: Probability and Odds, Part 4: Expected Outcomes and Judging Claims

cues.prompt: From past records, 4% of the parcels a courier delivers arrive late. How many of the next 650 parcels would you expect to arrive late?

m303-7-2.title: Probability of Combined Events, Part 1: Mutually Exclusive Events

cues.prompt: A jar holds 15 red, 9 blue and 6 green buttons. One button is taken at random. What is the probability that it is blue or green?
cues.working: There are $15 + 9 + 6 = 30$ buttons. Blue and green are mutually exclusive, so $\dfrac{9}{30} + \dfrac{6}{30} = \dfrac{15}{30} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

m303-7-2-b.title: Probability of Combined Events, Part 2: Independent Events

cues.prompt: One machine makes bolts, and 10% of them are too short. Another machine makes nuts, and 5% of them are cracked. One bolt and one nut are picked at random. What is the probability that the bolt is too short **and** the nut is cracked?
cues.working: The machines are independent, so $0.10 \times 0.05 = 0.005 = 0.5\%$.

m303-7-2-c.title: Probability of Combined Events, Part 3: Dependent Events

cues.prompt: A drawer holds 8 batteries, and 2 of them are dead. Two batteries are taken, one after the other, without putting the first back. What is the probability that both are dead?
cues.working: $\dfrac{2}{8} \times \dfrac{1}{7} = \dfrac{2}{56} = \dfrac{1}{28}$. After one dead battery is taken, 1 of the 7 left is dead.

m303-7-2-d.title: Probability of Combined Events, Part 4: At Least One and Exactly One

cues.prompt: A player makes 70% of free throws, and each shot is independent. The player takes 2 shots. What is the probability of making **exactly one**?
cues.working: Make then miss: $0.7 \times 0.3 = 0.21$. Miss then make: $0.3 \times 0.7 = 0.21$. Exactly one: $0.21 + 0.21 = 0.42 = 42\%$.

cues.prompt: A detailing business has fixed costs of \$1,800 a month. Each detail costs \$25 in supplies and sells for \$140. How many details must be sold each month to break even?
cues.working: Contribution: $140 - 25 = 115$. $1{,}800 \div 115 = 15.65\ldots$, so round up: 16 details.

m303-9-1.title: Logic Puzzles and Games, Part 1: Number Puzzles

cues.prompt: In a number pyramid, each brick is the sum of the two below it. The bottom row is $4$, $?$, $7$, and the top brick is $31$. What is the missing number?

m303-9-1-b.title: Logic Puzzles and Games, Part 2: Sudoku

cues.prompt: In a 4 × 4 Sudoku, one row holds $2$, $4$ and two empty cells. The column of the first empty cell already has a $1$. Which number goes in the first empty cell?
cues.working: The row is missing $1$ and $3$. The first empty cell’s column already has a $1$, so the first empty cell holds $3$ (and the second holds $1$).

m303-9-1-c.title: Logic Puzzles and Games, Part 3: KenKen

cues.prompt: In a 4 × 4 KenKen, using the numbers $1$ to $4$, which two-cell cage can be made **only one way**?
cues.working: $7+$ can only be $3 + 4$. But $5+$ can be $1 + 4$ or $2 + 3$; $1-$ can be $2 - 1$, $3 - 2$ or $4 - 3$; and $2\div$ can be $2 \div 1$ or $4 \div 2$.

m303-9-1-d.title: Logic Puzzles and Games, Part 4: Logic Grids

cues.prompt: Jin, Kate and Omar each drive a different vehicle: a truck, a van or a car. Kate does not drive the van or the car. Omar does not drive the van. Who drives the car?
cues.working: Kate drives neither the van nor the car, so Kate drives the truck. The van is not Kate’s or Omar’s, so Jin drives the van. That leaves the car for Omar.

m303-9-1-e.title: Logic Puzzles and Games, Part 5: Weighing Puzzles

cues.prompt: One of 9 coins is lighter than the others. What is the fewest number of weighings on a balance scale that is sure to find it?
cues.working: $9 = 3^2$. Weigh 3 against 3 with 3 left off: the light coin is in one group of 3. Then weigh 1 against 1 with 1 left off.

m303-9-1-f.title: Logic Puzzles and Games, Part 6: Crossing Puzzles

cues.prompt: Two adults and two children must cross a river. The boat carries two children or one adult, never an adult with a child. What is the fewest number of crossings that gets everyone across?
cues.working: Each adult takes the four-crossing pattern (both children over, one back, the adult over, the other child back): $4 + 4 = 8$. Then the two children cross together: $8 + 1 = 9$.

m303-9-1-g.title: Logic Puzzles and Games, Part 7: Take-Away Games

cues.prompt: Players take $1$, $2$ or $3$ counters a turn, and whoever takes the last counter wins. There are $15$ counters, and it is your turn. How many should you take?
cues.working: Leave a multiple of 4: $15 - 3 = 12$. Then take $4$ minus whatever your opponent takes.

m303-9-1-h.title: Logic Puzzles and Games, Part 8: Tic-Tac-Toe

cues.prompt: In tic-tac-toe, it is your turn. You cannot win on this move, but your opponent has two in a row with the third square empty. What should you do?
cues.working: Win first, then block, then fork. You cannot win, so block: otherwise your opponent completes the row on the next turn.
